Understanding Naval Architecture

Module 1 · Foundations

Foundations: weight, moments and pressure

Two simple ideas sit under almost everything in this guide. A weight placed away from a pivot creates a turning effect, a moment, and many weights act together through one point, the centre of gravity. And the pressure in a liquid grows steadily with depth, which is where buoyancy comes from. Trim, heel, stability, crane lifts, tank and bulkhead loads all follow from these two. New to the subject? Read this module first.

The question

Why does sliding one module a few metres along a 3,000 t barge make the whole barge tilt? And why can a thin pipe holding a bucketful of water burst the top off a tank?

1.1Weight, moments and the centre of gravity

A weight pulls straight down. If it sits away from a pivot, it also tries to turn things around that pivot, like a child on a see-saw. That turning effect is a : force × lever arm, where the is the sideways distance from the pivot to the line the force acts along. A 100 t load 10 m from midships has a moment of 1,000 tonne-metres; so does a 50 t load 20 m away.

When many weights act together, they behave exactly like one total weight acting through a single point, the (G). Its position is the moment-weighted average of all the individual positions: add up weight × position for every item and divide by the total weight. Naval architects do this sum, item by item, for every loading condition.

Why it matters everywhere

one idea, many uses

Weight off-centre along the length makes a vessel ; off-centre across the beam makes it list (Module 5). Weight high up lifts G and reduces stability (Module 4). A crane boom swung outboard creates a heeling moment. Bending in a hull girder is a moment too (Module 10).

Weight and mass

tonnes and kilonewtons

Mass is how much stuff there is (tonnes); weight is the force gravity puts on it (kilonewtons). One tonne weighs about 9.81 kN. Offshore people usually quote weights in tonnes and mean the weight of that mass; Module 13 (topic 13.6) untangles the units, and Units and conversions lists them all.

Balance

equilibrium

Something floating at rest is in balance twice over: its weight equals its buoyancy (no sinking or rising), and the two act along the same vertical line (no turning). Change either and the vessel moves until both balances are restored.

1.2Pressure grows with depth

is force per unit area. In a still liquid it comes from the weight of the liquid above: a square metre at 10 m depth in seawater carries the weight of 10 m³ of water, about 10 tonnes. So pressure grows in a straight line with depth: pressure = density × g × depth. It does not depend on how wide the sea or the tank is, only on how deep the point is.

Same in every direction

Pascal's principle

At any point in a still liquid the pressure pushes equally in all directions: down, up and sideways. That is why the sides and bottom of a hull, and even its overhanging parts, are all pushed inwards by the water around them. also explains hydraulics: pressure applied to a trapped liquid reaches every part of it.

Gauge and absolute

which zero?

is measured above the air's own pressure; adds the 1 bar of atmosphere on top. Most engineering on hulls and tanks uses gauge pressure, because the air pushes on both sides of a plate and cancels out.

Units, and "head"

kPa, bar, MPa, psi, metres

1 bar = 100 kPa = 0.1 MPa ≈ 14.5 psi ≈ the pressure of 10 m of seawater. Engineers often quote pressure simply as a : the height of liquid that would cause it ("5 m head"). A tank test to "2.4 m above the air pipe" is a pressure, written as a height.

Density matters

salt, fresh, oil, mud

Seawater is about 2.5% denser than fresh water, so a vessel floats about 2.5% deeper in a river or port of fresh water: the load line's fresh-water mark allows for it. Oil is lighter than water; drilling mud can be one and a half times heavier.

1.3Where buoyancy comes from

says a floating or submerged body is pushed up by the weight of the water it displaces. It is not a separate law: it is what you get when you add up the water pressure all over the hull. The sideways pushes on opposite sides cancel; the push up on the bottom, which is deeper, is larger than any push down on top.

Why a steel ship floats

A solid steel bolt displaces only its own small volume, so the water's upward push is about one-eighth of its weight (steel is about 7.7 times denser than seawater), and it sinks. Shape the same steel into a hull and it encloses a large volume of air. The hull sinks only until the water it pushes aside weighs as much as the whole vessel, and floats there. Floating is about the average density of everything inside the waterline, not the density of the material.

Offshore decision

The pressures here are the design loads for the hull plating itself: the bottom shell of a deep-draft hull is thicker because it carries more pressure. Watertight hatches, sea chests and subsea housings are all sized for the pressure at their depth, and pipelines and risers in deep water are checked for collapse under external pressure.

Misconception

"Heavy things sink, light things float." A 300,000 t tanker floats and a 50 g bolt sinks. What matters is whether the object's weight is less than the weight of water it can displace, which depends on its volume, so on its shape.

1.4Pressure on walls, tanks and bulkheads

On a vertical wall the pressure is zero at the liquid surface and greatest at the bottom, so the push forms a triangle. Its total is half the bottom pressure times the depth, and it acts a third of the way up from the bottom: the . The same applies to tank sides, flooded compartments, dock gates and dams.

1.5Only the height counts: air pipes and the hydrostatic paradox

Because pressure depends only on depth, a tall thin column of water produces the same pressure at its base as a wide lake of the same depth. This is the , and it has a very practical side. A ballast tank is vented through a thin . If the tank is overfilled and water rises up the pipe, the pressure inside the whole tank rises by the height of water in the pipe.

1.6Weight in water: lowering a load to the seabed

An object under water weighs less on the crane hook by the weight of water it displaces. Engineers call what remains its . For solid steel that is about 87% of its weight in air; for something with trapped air it can be negative, meaning it would float up.

Watch Animation on How 200,000 Tons of Steel Can Actually Float (Animations Xplaned) · How do ships float? Buoyancy! (learnbiologically) · more videos

What you should now understand

  • A moment is force × lever arm; all the weights on board act together through one point, the centre of gravity, found as a weighted average.
  • Pressure in still water = density × g × depth: about 1 bar for every 10 m of seawater, pushing equally in all directions.
  • Buoyancy is the sum of water pressure over the hull: the extra push on the deeper bottom. It equals the weight of water displaced.
  • A fully submerged body's buoyancy does not grow with depth; a floating body's grows with its draft.
  • Pressure on a wall forms a triangle: total force grows with depth squared and acts a third of the way up.
  • Only the height of liquid counts, not its amount: overfilling through an air pipe can burst a tank.
  • Under water, an object's hook load drops to its submerged weight; objects with trapped air can become buoyant.
In practice

Hydrostatic tables, stability booklets and loading computers are all built on these sums of pressure over the hull. Structural rules set plate thicknesses from the design pressure heads, tank tests fill tanks to a set head above the air pipe, and subsea lift plans list the weight in air, submerged weight and buoyancy of everything that goes overboard.

Module 2 · Vocabulary

Anatomy of a vessel

Before any calculation, learn the names. Every report, drawing and meeting uses them, and most of them describe a part that exists for a reason the later modules explain.

The question

An engineer says "the forepeak is pressed up, check the air pipe heads and the freeing ports before she sails." Which parts of the vessel is that, and why would anyone care?

2.1The parts of ships, barges and offshore platforms

2.2Four ways to read the drawing

Directions

bow · stern · port · starboard

Directions are fixed to the vessel, not the observer. Forward is towards the bow, aft towards the stern. Facing forward, port is on the left and starboard on the right. Lengthwise means fore-and-aft; crosswise means transverse.

The watertight envelope

shell · deck · closures

Shell plating, deck and the closures on every opening (hatch covers, manholes, air pipe heads) together make the sealed volume that floats the vessel. Every opening is a possible flooding route, so each has a rule-defined closure.

Subdivision

bulkheads · double bottom · tanks

Inside, bulkheads and the double bottom split the hull into compartments. One breach floods one space, not the whole hull, and the same compartments serve as ballast and fuel tanks.

Structure

plating · stiffeners · girders

The cross-section shows the hull as a beam: plates carry the load, stiffeners stop them buckling, and floors and girders tie the bottom together. Module 10 shows how it bends.

2.3Filling and emptying the tanks: the ballast system

Ships ballast with the sea itself: are filled with seawater drawn in through the hull and emptied by pumping it back overboard. A small plant of openings, pipes, valves and pumps does this, run from a control console. How fast it can move water matters: load-out plans check pump rates against the tide (Module 5), and crane vessels shift water between wing tanks as the crane slews (topic 5.3).

Sea chest and sea valve

the way in

A recessed box in the bottom or side shell, below the waterline and covered by a grating. A sea valve just inside closes it. Sea valves are among the few openings in the hull below the waterline, so they are inspected closely.

Filling

gravity first, then the pump

A tank below the waterline fills by itself once its valve is open: the sea's pressure pushes water in until the level inside reaches the waterline (Module 1). The pump speeds this up and is needed for tanks higher up, such as topside tanks.

Emptying

always pumped

Water in a tank below the waterline cannot drain out by itself; the sea would push it straight back. The pump sucks it out through a pipe ending near the tank bottom and discharges it overboard above the waterline. A small takes the last few centimetres the main pump cannot reach.

Control

valves, levels, rates

The crew chooses tanks by opening and closing remotely operated valves, and watches each tank's level on gauges or by sounding. Air pipes let air out as a tank fills and back in as it empties. Ship pumps typically move hundreds to a few thousand cubic metres an hour.

Barges

portable pumps

A dumb barge has no engine room, so for a load-out temporary pumps are set up on deck or on the quay, often submersible pumps lowered through the manholes, with hoses to each tank. That is why barge procedures check manholes, air pipes and sounding pipes so closely.

Ballast water treatment

environmental rules

Ballast taken on in one port and released in another can carry organisms across oceans; invasive species have spread this way. Under the IMO Ballast Water Management Convention (in force since 2017), ships now before discharge, usually by filtering plus UV light or electrolysis.

Why so many parts?

Each part answers one of three needs: stay afloat (watertight envelope and reserve buoyancy), stay upright (low weights, ballast tanks, freeing ports that shed water from the deck), and stay in one piece (plating, stiffeners and girders sized for wave loads).

Offshore decision

Transport plans name parts constantly: where the grillage sits over the bulkheads, which ballast tanks are filled, where the bridle connects, whether the emergency towline is rigged. Surveyors check the closures (manholes, air pipes, sounding pipes) before a tow leaves.

Misconception

"A barge is just a floating steel box." From outside, yes. Inside, it is divided into many tanks by bulkheads, stiffened by frames and girders, and fitted with raked ends, skegs and towing gear. All of these decide how it floats, tows and carries load.

What you should now understand

  • Bow, stern, port, starboard, fore-and-aft and amidships are fixed to the vessel.
  • The hull is a watertight envelope (shell plating, deck, closures) divided inside by bulkheads and a double bottom.
  • Tanks low in the hull (double bottom, peaks, wings) hold ballast to control draft, trim and heel.
  • Ballast tanks fill from the sea through a sea chest, by gravity or pump, and are always pumped out; valves on the ballast main pick the tank, and air pipes let the air out and in.
  • Every opening in the deck (hatches, vents, air pipes, manholes) has a closure, because each is a route for water into the reserve buoyancy.
  • A barge has no engine or rudder; raked ends, skegs and towing gear make it tow well.
  • A fixed jacket platform is a piled steel truss carrying topsides clear of the waves (the air gap). In deep water an FPSO floats instead, turning around its turret while moorings hold it and risers bring the flow up from subsea wells.
In practice

The opening question decoded: the forepeak ballast tank at the bow is filled right to the top ("pressed up", so it has no free surface), and before sailing someone confirms that the closing heads on the tank vents work and that the openings in the bulwarks can drain water off the deck. Each check protects either reserve buoyancy or stability, the subjects of the next two modules.

Module 3 · Hydrostatics

Buoyancy, displacement, draft and freeboard

Everything offshore starts with one balance: the water pushes up exactly as hard as the vessel pushes down. Draft, freeboard and load capacity all follow from it.

The question

A 2,000-tonne steel barge floats. A 2,000-tonne solid block of the same steel sinks straight to the seabed. What is different?

3.1Same steel, different shape

Water pushes on every submerged surface. The pressure grows with depth, so the push on the bottom is larger than the push on the top. The net upward result is , and it always equals the weight of the water that the object has pushed aside. This is .

A solid block can only push aside its own small volume of water: about one-eighth of its own weight for steel. A hollow of the same steel can push aside far more water, because the air inside takes up space without adding much weight.

Foundations: 1.3 Where buoyancy comes from: water pressure on the hull · 1.1 Moments and the centre of gravity

3.2The floating balance: draft and freeboard

Why it happens

A floating vessel sinks until it has pushed aside water weighing exactly as much as itself. Adding cargo means more water must be pushed aside, so the hull sits deeper.

A wider hull has more , so each centimetre of extra immersion pushes aside more water. It therefore needs less extra immersion for the same added load. That rate is called .

Offshore decision

Before a barge is loaded with a jacket, module or spool, engineers check the resulting against the water depth at the quay and on the route, and the remaining against the risk of green water on deck and the reserve buoyancy needed for stability (Module 4).

Misconception

"Heavy things sink, light things float." Floating depends on how much water an object can displace, which depends on its total enclosed volume, not on whether its material is heavy. Steel ships float; a small steel bolt sinks.

Optional detail: the arithmetic behind the experiment

For a box-shaped barge of length L, beam B and draft T in water of density ρ:

Displacement Δ = ρ · L · B · T   ⇒   T = Δ / (ρ · L · B)

TPC = ρ · Awp / 100 = ρ · L · B / 100   (tonnes per cm)

Example: 60 m × 20 m barge in seawater: TPC = 1.025 × 1,200 / 100 = 12.3 t/cm, so 100 t of extra cargo sinks it about 8 cm. At 10 m beam the same 100 t sinks it about 16 cm.

Real hulls are not boxes: naval architects use computed from the hull geometry to look up displacement, TPC and other values at each draft.

Easily confused terms: 13.5 Where it is measured from

3.3Displacement is not capacity, and it is not tonnage

Three similar-sounding measures appear in vessel data sheets. Only one of them is a weight of the vessel itself.

Displacement

tonnes (mass)

The mass of water the hull pushes aside, which equals the total mass of the floating vessel and everything on it. It changes every time you load, ballast or burn fuel.

Lightship and deadweight

tonnes (mass)

is the empty vessel. is everything you can add (cargo, ballast, fuel, stores) at a given draft. Displacement = lightship + deadweight.

Internal capacity

cubic metres (volume)

How much space is inside tanks, holds or on deck. A tank can have plenty of volume left while the vessel has run out of deadweight, and the reverse.

Gross / net tonnage

dimensionless index

A regulatory measure of enclosed volume used for fees, manning and rules. Despite the name, is not a weight.

Easily confused terms: 13.6 Mass, force and volume

3.4Floating versus held underwater

Use the "Held underwater" mode in the barge experiment above. When a hull is pushed fully under, it displaces its whole volume, so buoyancy becomes larger than its weight. Something (a hold-down line, a pile, a crane) must supply the difference. Release it, and the hull rises until the balance is restored.

This matters offshore whenever a buoyant object is held submerged: buoyancy modules on risers, subsea structures during lowering, tension-leg platforms, or a pipeline being kept on the seabed by its weight coating.

3.5The load line mark: how deep is too deep

Freeboard is the vessel's reserve: buoyancy above the water for waves, damage and heel, and height to keep the sea off the deck. Overloading spends that reserve where nobody can see it. The makes the limit visible: a ring and bar painted on both sides amidships, with a short ladder of lines beside it. Whatever the vessel carries, the line for its zone, season and water must never be under water.

The painted shapes are the same size on every ship: a 20 m coaster carries the same 300 mm ring as a 400 m container ship. What changes is where the ring sits (the ship's assigned summer freeboard below the deck line) and how far apart the lines are, which follows the ship's own draught and displacement.

The mark was a hard-won reform. In 19th-century Britain, overloaded and over-insured "coffin ships" sank with their crews; the campaigner Samuel Plimsoll forced a compulsory mark into law in 1876, which is why it is still called the Plimsoll line. Today the International Convention on Load Lines (1966, amended by its 1988 Protocol) applies to almost every ship of 24 m or more on international voyages.

MarkNameWhere it isUse it when
Deck line300 × 25 mm bar; its top edge is level with the top of the freeboard deck at the sideThe datum: every freeboard is measured down from its top edge
Ring and barLoad line mark (Plimsoll disc)Ring 300 mm across, 25 mm thick; bar 450 mm long through its centre. The centre sits the summer freeboard below the deck line, amidshipsIts bar marks the summer line in seawater. The letters beside it name the authority that assigned the freeboard (for example LR, AB, NV)
SSummerTop edge level with the centre of the ringSummer zones and seasons, in seawater
TTropical1/48 of the summer draught above STropical zones: calmer, so a little less freeboard
WWinter1/48 of the summer draught below SWinter seasonal zones: rougher, so more freeboard
WNAWinter North Atlantic50 mm below W; only on ships up to 100 m longCrossing the North Atlantic in winter, the roughest common route
FFresh waterFresh water allowance (FWA) above S, on the aft sideSummer loading in fresh water: she will rise to S on reaching the sea
TFTropical freshFWA above T, on the aft sideTropical loading in fresh water

Why the lines step

The summer freeboard is the baseline. Calmer seas allow a little less reserve (T), rougher ones demand more (W, WNA). The fresh-water lines are not about weather at all: fresh water is less dense, so the same ship floats deeper in it. Loading to F in a river port leaves her exactly at S once she reaches seawater.

Offshore decision

Barges and heavy transport vessels carry load line certificates too. A marine warranty surveyor checks that the loaded draught for the tow, including ballast, seafastening and any water trapped on deck, leaves the vessel above its line for the zone and season of the route. Cargo that overhangs or sits above the freeboard deck may need a special or one-voyage exemption from the flag state.

Misconception

"The Plimsoll line shows the draught." It shows a limit, not a reading. Draught is read from the at bow, stern and amidships. The load line says how far down those readings may go, and it may legally be under water in fresh or brackish water.

How the summer freeboard is set

length · type · corrections

The rules start from a table freeboard that grows with ship length. Type A ships (tankers: liquid cargo, small, gas-tight openings, high subdivision) get less than Type B (everything else). The figure is then corrected: up for full hulls (block coefficient above 0.68) and for depth greater than L/15; down for enclosed superstructures and sheer that add reserve buoyancy. A minimum bow height keeps the forecastle out of head seas.

Conditions of assignment

the openings must be tight

A freeboard only counts if water cannot get in above it. So the same rules fix the strength of hatch covers, the sill heights of doors, the height of (760 mm on the freeboard deck) and ventilators, the area of in bulwarks, and guard rails for the crew. Module 2 shows where each one is.

Zones and seasons

a world chart

The Convention's chart divides the oceans into tropical zones, summer zones and seasonal areas whose rule changes with the date: winter in the North Atlantic from October to April, for example. A voyage plan checks the line for every zone on the route; a ship leaving the tropics must be light enough for the next zone by the time she enters it.

Timber load lines

LS · LT · LW · LF · LTF

Ships certified to carry timber stowed solidly on deck get a second ladder, prefixed L, on the aft side. A well-secured timber deck cargo adds buoyancy and keeps seas off the deck, so the rules allow it a little less freeboard.

Certificate and surveys

5-year certificate, annual checks

The International Load Line Certificate records the assigned freeboards and the FWA. It is renewed every five years, with annual surveys to confirm that the marks and every closing appliance are still as approved. Ports can detain a ship found loaded beyond her mark.

Barges

simple hull, simple rules

An unmanned barge with only small deck openings closed watertight is a low-risk hull, and the rules allow it a reduced freeboard. That is one reason a deck barge such as the one in 14.2 can load to only about 1.2 m of freeboard, and why water on deck and open manholes worry tow surveyors so much.

Optional detail: line spacing, fresh and dock water allowances

With summer draught TS, summer displacement Δ (t, in seawater) and TPC (t/cm, at the summer waterline):

T line = S + TS/48  ·  W line = S − TS/48  ·  WNA = W − 50 mm

Fresh water allowance FWA (cm) = Δ ÷ (40 × TPC)

Dock water allowance DWA = FWA × (1,025 − ρdock) ÷ 25   (ρ in kg/m³)

For the example ship: TS/48 = 6,000 ÷ 48 = 125 mm; FWA = 6,600 ÷ (40 × 12.5) = 13.2 cm = 132 mm. Loading in brackish dock water of 1,010 kg/m³ she may submerge her line by 132 × 15 ÷ 25 ≈ 79 mm, which at 12.5 t/cm is about 99 t of extra cargo.

Where the 40 comes from: in fresh water the same mass Δ needs more volume, Δ/1.000 − Δ/1.025 = 0.025 Δ ÷ 1.025 m³. Each centimetre of sinkage adds TPC ÷ 1.025 m³. Divide one by the other and the 1.025s cancel: sinkage = 0.025 Δ ÷ TPC = Δ ÷ (40 × TPC) cm. The DWA scales this linearly for water between fresh and salt.

Easily confused terms: 13.5 Where it is measured from · Parts named: Module 2 · Anatomy of a vessel

Watch Animation on How 200,000 Tons of Steel Can Actually Float (Animations Xplaned) · How do ships float? Buoyancy! (learnbiologically) · more videos

What you should now understand

  • Buoyancy equals the weight of water displaced. A freely floating vessel settles where that equals its total weight.
  • Draft is how deep the hull sits; freeboard is how much hull remains above water. Adding weight increases draft and reduces freeboard.
  • A wider waterplane needs less extra immersion per tonne added (higher TPC).
  • Displacement (a mass), capacity (a volume) and tonnage (an index) are different things.
  • The load line mark sets the minimum freeboard: one line per zone and season, with fresh-water lines because ships float deeper in fresh water.
In practice

Every tow, transport and installation study starts with a and a hydrostatic check: will the barge or vessel float at an acceptable draft and freeboard with the payload, ballast and seafastening on board? These numbers feed the stability, motion and structural checks in the later modules.

Module 4 · Intact stability

Stability: the tendency to return upright

Floating is only the first test. A vessel must also push itself back upright when a wave, the wind or a moving load tips it over. That depends on where its weight sits and how its underwater shape changes as it heels.

The question

A barge carries a tall module whose centre of gravity is well above the waterline. Will it come back upright after a gust heels it, or keep going over?

4.1Two points and two forces

All the vessel's weight acts as if concentrated at one point, the . All the buoyancy acts through the centre of the underwater volume, the . Upright and at rest, G and B sit on the same vertical line, so the two equal forces cancel.

When the vessel , G stays fixed in the hull (unless something moves), but the underwater shape changes: one side immerses and the other emerges, so B moves towards the low side. Now weight and buoyancy act along different vertical lines. The horizontal distance between them is the , measured in metres: draw a horizontal line from G to the buoyancy line, and Z is where it meets it. It is small, typically centimetres to a metre or two even for a very stable barge. The vessel's total weight (its : hull, cargo, ballast, fuel and everything else on board, which for a floating vessel equals the weight of water its underwater volume pushes aside) × GZ is the , the turning effect that pushes the vessel back. It is measured in tonne-metres (or kN·m): a 3,000 t barge with GZ = 0.5 m has a righting moment of 1,500 t·m. The underwater shape matters through GZ, not through the force: it decides where B is and how far it moves as the vessel heels.

That can sound backwards: if buoyancy moves to the low side, why doesn't it push the vessel further over? Because buoyancy pushes up, not sideways. An upward push on the side that has dipped lifts it back, while the weight, now acting on the high side of B, pulls that side down. Like a see-saw pushed up at its low end, the vessel turns back towards upright. The extra buoyancy comes from the wedge of hull that has gone under on the low side; the wedge that has come out of the water on the high side loses the same amount. The vessel only capsizes if G ends up beyond B, so that weight acts on the low side instead.

Why it happens

Raising cargo raises G. B moves sideways by the same amount whatever the cargo height, but a higher G also moves sideways further when the hull tilts. Once G's sideways movement catches up with B's, the righting lever disappears.

The , is the height that tells you where that crossover happens for small angles. While G is below M, the vessel is initially stable, even with G above B.

Offshore decision

Before a transport, engineers compute the full with the actual cargo, ballast and wind area, then check it against the stability criteria of the applicable rules and the marine warranty surveyor. A tall, heavy deck cargo can be the deciding factor in barge selection.

Misconceptions

  • "Buoyancy moving to the low side pushes it further over." Buoyancy acts upwards, so on the low side it lifts the side that has dipped. The danger is G moving out beyond B, not B moving out.
  • "If it floats, it's stable." Floating is about vertical balance; stability is about turning balance. The unstable preset floats perfectly well.
  • "G above B means it will capsize." Most ships have G above B. Stability only needs G below M.
  • "More GM is always better." High GM gives a quick, jerky roll that is hard on crew, cargo lashings and equipment.
Optional detail: KB, BM, KM, GM and the small-angle formula

Heights are measured from the K. For a box of beam B and draft T:

KB = T/2    BM = I / ∇ = B² / (12 T)    KM = KB + BM    GM = KM − KG

I is the second moment of area of the waterplane about the centreline and ∇ is the displaced volume. A wider waterplane gives a much larger BM (it grows with beam squared), which is why wide barges are so stable.

For small angles: GZ ≈ GM · sin φ     Roll period Tφ ≈ 2π k / √(g · GM)

k is the radius of gyration in roll, including the water that moves with the hull. The second formula is why high GM gives a short, snappy roll period.

For a wall-sided box before the deck edge goes under, the exact result is GZ = sin φ (GM + ½ BM tan² φ). That extra term is why a box with slightly negative GM finds an angle of loll instead of capsizing.

4.2Small angles versus large angles

GM describes only the first few degrees: it is the slope of the GZ curve at the origin (the dashed tangent line in the chart above). At larger angles, the deck edge goes underwater or the bilge comes out, the waterplane shape changes, and the curve bends away from the tangent. Two vessels with the same GM can have very different large-angle behaviour.

The useful information is in the whole curve: the largest righting lever, the angle where it occurs, the where it falls to zero, and the area under the curve, which is the energy available to resist a gust or a wave. That area is in metre-radians (m·rad): metres of lever times angle in radians; multiplied by the displacement it becomes energy. Rules and warranty guidelines set criteria on these features, and on wind heeling, because a single GM value is not a complete measure of safety.

Easily confused terms: 13.1 Heel, list, loll and roll

4.3What makes a hull stable: beam, height of weight and freeboard

A designer has three main levers. Beam sets how far B can move sideways as the hull heels, so a wider hull pushes back harder. The height of the weight sets where G is: lower is better. Freeboard, the height of the deck above the water, sets how far the hull can heel before the deck edge goes under and the righting lever starts to collapse. Change one at a time below and compare the new GZ curve with the original (dashed).

Beam

the strongest lever

Initial stability grows with beam squared. This is why barges, which are very wide for their draft, are so stiff, and why narrow hulls carry ballast low down.

Height of weight

keep heavy things low

Every tonne lifted raises G. Tall deck cargo, cranes and heavy topsides push G up; ballast in the double bottom pulls it down. Lifting a load with a crane effectively moves its weight to the crane tip (Module 5).

Freeboard

range of stability

Freeboard hardly changes GM, but it sets how far the vessel can heel before the deck goes under. More freeboard means a longer, fuller GZ curve and more reserve against capsize. Openings in the hull and deck matter for the same reason: once they go under, water gets in (the downflooding angle).

Watch Why Don't Cruise Ships Tip Over? An introduction to ship stability (Casual Navigation) · Metacentric Height, Ship’s Equilibrium, Angle of Loll, Righting Lever and Righting Moment (Nautical Academy) · Transverse statical stability of ships: GM, KM, GZ and RM (Steering Mariners) · more videos

What you should now understand

  • G is where weight acts; B is where buoyancy acts. Heeling moves B towards the low side, and the gap between the two lines of action (GZ) creates the righting moment.
  • Raising weight raises G and reduces stability. Stability needs G below the metacentre M, not below B.
  • GM is the small-angle slope of the GZ curve. Large-angle safety needs the whole curve.
  • Higher GM means a quicker, harsher roll; lower GM a slow, gentle roll with less margin.
  • Beam gives initial stiffness, low weight gives everything, and freeboard gives range: how far the vessel can heel and still come back.
In practice

Stability checks for barge transports and installation vessels compare the GZ curve, including wind heeling and the effect of crane lifts, against the criteria of the governing rules and the . The inputs are the weight and G estimates from Module 3; the risks are G creeping up as the design develops and openings that would flood at large angles.

Module 5 · Loading conditions

Trim, heel, ballast and the free-surface effect

Where weight sits along and across the hull decides how the vessel floats: level, bow-down, or leaning to one side. Ballast water is the tool for correcting it, and liquid that can slosh is a hidden threat to stability.

The question

A 1,200 t module is skidded onto the forward end of a transport barge. The bow dips. How do we bring the barge back to an , and what could go wrong while we do it?

5.1Loading a barge

Weight placed forward of the centre of buoyancy makes the barge by the bow; weight placed off the centreline makes it . Filling tanks on the opposite side or end creates a balancing moment.

Why it happens

Adding weight increases displacement, so the barge sinks bodily (mean draft rises) and also trims or heels if the weight is off-centre. Moving weight leaves displacement unchanged: mean draft stays the same, only the trim, heel and G move.

Ballast corrects trim and heel by adding an opposing moment, at the cost of extra displacement and draft.

Offshore decision

During a , the module moves from quay to barge in stages over hours while the tide changes. Engineers prepare a ballast plan that keeps the barge level with the quay at each stage, and check pump capacity, tank limits and the free-surface effect of the tanks being worked.

Misconception

"Ballast water always improves stability." Ballast low in the hull lowers G, which helps. But a partly filled tank has a that shifts as the vessel heels, which reduces effective stability. Ballasting can make things worse while tanks are partly full.

Optional detail: trim, heel and the free-surface correction

Trim angle ≈ (Δ · LCG) / (Δ · GML)   Heel angle ≈ (Δ · TCG) / (Δ · GMT)

GML is the longitudinal metacentric height. For a long hull it is many times larger than GMT, which is why a weight shift that would heel a barge several degrees only trims it a fraction of a degree.

Free-surface correction FSC = ρliquid · i / Δ    with i = l · b³ / 12 for a rectangular tank

The effective GM is GMsolid − FSC. The tank width b is cubed, so wide tanks are far worse than narrow ones. That is why tanks are subdivided by longitudinal .

Easily confused terms: 13.1 Heel, list, loll and roll · 13.2 Trim and pitch

5.2Empty, partly filled and full tanks

The experiment moves the liquid slowly. In waves it also surges from side to side and end to end. This slams into tank walls and tops with impact pressures, and it moves the liquid's weight around faster than the free-surface sum assumes, worst when its natural period is close to the vessel's roll or pitch period. Six defences, from the most used to the least:

Full or empty

no free surface

A tank pressed full has no surface to move; an empty one has nothing to move. Ballast plans keep slack tanks to as few, and for as short a time, as possible. This is the main rule.

Subdivide

narrower tanks

split a wide tank into narrow ones. Free-surface loss goes with width cubed, so two halves have a quarter of the effect between them, and a narrow tank sloshes at a short period, clear of the roll.

Wash bulkheads and baffles

calm the flow

are plates with large holes: the tank still fills and drains as one, but the moving water is broken up and loses energy. Web frames and girders inside a tank do the same. They do not reduce the free-surface loss of GM, because the liquid still finds its level across the whole tank as the vessel heels.

Avoid resonant fill levels

fill limits

A tank's sloshing period depends on its length and the liquid depth. Where it would match the vessel's motions, fill levels are restricted: membrane LNG carriers, for example, typically may not sail between about 10% and 70% full, because sloshing impacts could damage the tank lining.

Design for the impacts

where it cannot be avoided

Tank corners, tops and internal structure are strengthened for sloshing pressures, which are found from model tests or CFD and checked like any other local load (Module 10).

Use it on purpose

anti-roll tanks

An is tuned so its water sloshes at the roll period, lagging the roll by a quarter of a cycle, so it pushes against the motion instead of adding to it (topic 9.4).

5.3A crane lift, stage by stage

The moment a crane lifts a load clear of the deck, the load's weight effectively acts at the crane's boom tip, high above the deck, because the load is free to swing from the hook. G rises immediately, as if the load had been teleported to the tip. Slewing the boom over the side then adds a large heeling moment. Each stage changes the stability picture, and the most critical stage is not always the obvious one.

Why it happens

A suspended load acts at its suspension point, so lifting it raises G as much as moving it to the boom tip would. Slewing moves that effective weight outboard, which heels the vessel. Counter-ballast cancels the heeling moment, but it is slow to move and it stays behind when the load is released.

Offshore decision

Lift plans assess every stage: lift-off, slew, crossing, lowering, set-down and the sudden release. Each has its own heel, stability margin and dynamic hook load, and the ballast sequence is planned to stay safe throughout.

Misconception

"The heaviest moment is the dangerous one." Release can be the critical stage: losing the load's moment suddenly while counter-ballast is still in place can roll the vessel sharply the other way.

Easily confused terms: 13.3 Static versus dynamic loads

Watch Ship Stability: Angle of List. How does a ship capsize? (Saurav Saini) · Stability Part 9: Free Surface Effect (Waterborne Marine Publication and Education) · Ship stability focused on free surface effects, metacentric height, loss of GM and liquid sloshing (Ship Ahoy Vlogs) · more videos

What you should now understand

  • Trim and heel come from weight off the centre of buoyancy, lengthwise and sideways.
  • Adding weight changes displacement and mean draft; moving weight only changes trim, heel and G.
  • A partly filled tank reduces effective GM through its free surface, even though no weight is added or raised.
  • Sloshing in slack tanks adds impact loads; tanks are kept full or empty, subdivided, baffled with wash bulkheads, or kept away from resonant fill levels. Wash bulkheads calm the surge but do not reduce the free-surface loss.
  • A suspended load acts at the hook's suspension point. Lifts must be checked stage by stage, including release.
In practice

Load-out and ballast plans, transport loading conditions and crane-vessel lift stability are typical deliverables. The analysis tracks displacement, trim, heel and GM (including free-surface corrections) for each stage, using the vessel's stability booklet or a hydrostatic model.

Module 6 · Metocean

Waves, wind, currents and sea states

The environment is the load. Engineers describe it with a handful of statistics, and a lot of the judgement in offshore work lies in choosing which conditions to analyse.

The question

The forecast says "3 m waves". Is that a gentle swell or a dangerous sea for a barge tow? What else do you need to know?

6.1Anatomy of a regular wave

A is a perfectly repeating train, the idealisation engineers start from. It has a (trough to crest), a (seconds between crests passing a fixed point), a (crest to crest) and a direction. In deep water, period alone sets the wavelength and speed: longer-period waves are longer and faster.

Why it happens

A wave is energy moving through the water. Each water particle is pushed up, forward, down and back in a loop, then hands the motion on to the next. That is why a floating object bobs and sways but is not carried along with the crests.

The motion fades with depth: at half a wavelength down it is only about 4% of the surface motion. Topic 6.2 looks inside the wave in more detail.

Offshore decision

Particle motion with depth determines how far wave loads reach down a jacket or riser, and how quiet it is at the seabed for a subsea installation. Long-period swell reaches much deeper than short wind waves of the same height.

Misconception

"Waves are water rushing towards the shore." The wave form travels at speed, but water particles mostly circulate in place. Currents, not waves, transport water over distance.

Optional detail: deep-water relationships

Wavelength λ = g T² / 2π ≈ 1.56 T²   (metres, T in seconds)

Crest speed c = λ / T ≈ 1.56 T   (m/s)    Orbit radius at depth z: r(z) = (H/2) · e−2πz/λ

A 10 s wave is about 156 m long and travels at about 15.6 m/s (30 knots). In shallower water (depth less than about half a wavelength), waves slow down, shorten and steepen, and the orbits flatten into ellipses.

6.2How the water actually moves

A wave is a shape, and energy, travelling across the surface. The water it passes through mostly stays where it is: each small traces a loop and comes back almost to where it started. A parcel has no physical boundary: it is an imaginary blob drawn around some water and allowed to move and deform with it, so it always holds the same water, like a drop of dye. It is small enough to move with a single velocity (a metre or so under a 150 m wave), yet large enough to hold billions of molecules, so it behaves like smooth water. Its shape squashes and stretches as the wave passes, but its volume stays the same, because water is almost incompressible. Below, every dot is one parcel of water, drawn at its centre. The orange line is a column of dye injected straight down, and the dashed line is a row of dye at one depth. Watch what they do as crests pass.

1. Loops, not rivers

orbital motion

Each parcel moves up and forward as a crest arrives, then down and back as the trough follows. In deep water the path is a circle the size of the wave height at the surface. The parcel hands its motion on to the next one, so the energy travels and the water stays.

2. Forward under crests, backward under troughs

velocity

The water moves with the wave under a crest and against it under a trough. Its speed is small compared with the wave: about π × height ÷ wavelength of the crest speed, typically 5–15%. A 5 m, 8 s wave runs at 12 m/s; its water moves at under 2 m/s.

3. Fading with depth

the wave's "roots"

The loops shrink exponentially going down: to about 4% of their surface size at half a wavelength. Long-period swell reaches far deeper than short wind waves, which is why a 15 s swell can stir the seabed in 100 m of water while a storm of short waves cannot.

4. Shallow water: the seabed joins in

ellipses and sloshing

When the depth is less than about half a wavelength, the bottom stops the vertical motion. The loops flatten into ellipses, and right at the seabed the water just sloshes back and forth. The wave slows down, shortens, and steepens: this is why waves pile up and break on beaches, and why seabed pipelines need on-bottom stability checks.

5. Loops that do not quite close

Stokes drift

The forward motion at the top of each loop happens slightly higher up, where the motion is a little stronger, than the backward motion at the bottom. So each loop ends a little ahead of where it started, and surface water creeps slowly in the direction of the waves. Floating debris, oil and lifeboats drift this way, as well as with wind and current.

6. Energy travels slower than the crests

group velocity

Waves come in groups. In deep water a group, and the energy it carries, travels at half the speed of the crests: crests appear at the back of a group, move through it and fade out at the front. Swell from a distant storm arrives at the group speed, longest periods first. Groups of big waves also drive the slow drift of moored vessels (Module 11).

Why it happens

Under a crest there is more water overhead, so the pressure is a little higher than under a trough at the same depth (Module 1). Water is pushed from high pressure towards low: forward and up ahead of the crest, back and down behind it. Gravity then pulls the raised water down again, and the cycle repeats one wavelength further on. The water is a messenger, not a passenger.

When a wave gets too steep, about one-seventh of its length, the water at the crest moves faster than the crest itself. It outruns the wave shape, tumbles forward and the wave breaks. Only then is water carried forward in bulk, which is why breaking waves and green water hit structures so hard.

Offshore decision

Wave loads on jacket legs, braces and risers come from these water velocities and accelerations (wave "kinematics"), which is why they are largest near the surface and smaller lower down. Seabed velocities decide whether pipelines and cables stay put and whether sediment scours around foundations. Crest velocities set slamming and green water loads; group statistics set slow-drift motions of moored vessels.

Misconception

"A 12 m/s wave hits a structure at 12 m/s." The wave shape travels at 12 m/s, but the water that actually pushes on a jacket leg moves much more slowly, typically one or two metres per second. Except in a breaking wave, the force comes from the water rocking to and fro, not from a wall of water arriving at the wave's speed.

Optional detail: dispersion, group speed and drift

ω² = g·k·tanh(k·h)    with ω = 2π/T, k = 2π/λ, h = water depth

Crest speed c = ω/k    Group speed cg = ½ c (1 + 2kh / sinh 2kh): ½ c in deep water, → c in shallow water

Surface water speed ≈ ω·H/2    Stokes drift at the surface (deep water) ≈ ω·k·(H/2)²

In shallow water (depth below about a twentieth of a wavelength) all wave periods travel at the same speed, √(g·h). That is the speed of a tsunami: about 200 m/s (700 km/h) over 4,000 m of ocean.

6.3Same height, different period

The short-period sea is steep: a 90 m barge spans more than one whole wave, so it is slammed and pitched in a choppy way. The long-period swell is gentle to look at, but the whole barge rides up and down each wave, and long periods can match a large vessel's natural roll or heave periods (Module 7). Height alone does not describe a sea.

A is generated by local wind: short, steep and confused. has travelled from distant storms: long, regular and often from a different direction.

6.4Where waves come from

Every wave needs two things: something to put energy in, and something to pull the water back to level. At sea the energy almost always comes from the wind. (A ship's wake, an earthquake and the tide are the other sources.) The pull back is gravity: raised water falls, overshoots and rises again, which is the cycle described in 6.2.

Gravity explains why the water oscillates, but not how fast. A guitar string has a fixed length, so it can only sound a few notes. The sea surface has no edges, so it can carry a wave of any length. Each length has its own period (λ ≈ 1.56 T² in deep water). The water supplies that rule. The wind decides which periods are actually made, and how big, through three things: its speed, the distance of open water it blows over (the ), and how long it has been blowing.

1. The source sets the period

free variables

Period, height and direction are set where the wave is made. For a wind sea, the free inputs are the wind's speed, fetch and duration. Hs and Tp are results, not inputs.

2. The water sets length and speed

dependent variables

Once the period and water depth are known, the dispersion relation (6.2) fixes the wavelength, crest speed and group speed. The orbits then follow from the height and wavelength. Water cannot choose a different wavelength for the same period.

3. Period survives the journey

conserved

Crests are neither created nor lost between two points, so they pass each point at the same rate. As a wave moves into shallow water its wavelength and speed change, but its period does not. The period is set at birth.

4. Height is a separate dial

independent of period

In linear theory, height and period are unrelated, which is why 6.3 can compare two 4 m seas. The only link is breaking: a wave steeper than about 1 in 7 cannot exist. In a wind sea, both grow together because the same wind is feeding them.

5. Long waves outrun short ones

dispersion

A wave is water swinging under gravity, like a pendulum. A longer pendulum swings more slowly but its bob moves faster. Likewise a 400 m wave has twice the period of a 100 m one (16 s against 8 s) but covers four times the distance per swing, so it travels twice as fast. Its energy moves at half the crest speed, about 0.78 × T m/s. Over 1,000 km, 16 s swell arrives after about 22 hours and 8 s swell after about 44.

6. Short waves fade on the way

dissipation

Short storm waves are steep, so once the wind stops they keep breaking as whitecaps; long ones of the same height are too gentle to break. Short waves also go through more cycles per kilometre (about 10,000 for an 8 s wave over 1,000 km, against 2,500 at 16 s), losing a little energy each time. Friction in the water kills a ripple in about a second but barely touches long swell, which can cross whole oceans. A distant coast therefore sees the long, regular part of a messy storm sea.

7. A ship's wake shows the chain

source speed → wave

A ship's wave pattern travels with it, so the crest speed equals the ship's speed. That fixes the wavelength (2π × speed² ÷ g) and the period. At 12 knots, the waves are about 24 m long with a period of about 4 s. This is the wave-making part of resistance (Module 8).

Why it happens

Gusts dent the calm surface into ripples. The wind then pushes harder on the back of each wave than on its sheltered front, so it feeds energy into any wave moving slower than itself. Short waves soon get too steep and break as whitecaps. Interactions between waves pass energy to slightly longer, faster ones, so the peak period keeps rising.

Growth stops when the biggest waves run about as fast as the wind (in practice a little faster). The wind can no longer push them. That ceiling ties the period to the wind speed: Tp ≈ 0.8 × wind speed in m/s, with Hs ≈ 0.025 × wind speed². A 10 m/s wind gives about 8.3 s and 2.5 m; 20 m/s gives about 16.6 s and 9.9 m. Double the wind and you double the period and quadruple the height.

Offshore decision

Wave forecasts and the hindcasts behind a metocean basis come from computing waves from wind fields, using this physics in spectral wave models. For a marine operation, a calm local day is no guarantee: swell from a storm 1,000 km or more away can arrive with no local wind at all, longest periods first. Sheltered sites with short fetches only get short, low wind seas, even in strong wind.

Misconception

"No wind, so no waves." The local wind sets only the wind sea. Swell is made elsewhere, sometimes days earlier, and it can be the largest and longest-period part of the sea on a windless day. Long-period swell is exactly what excites the slow natural motions of large vessels (Module 7).

Optional detail: what is free and what follows

Free (set by the source): period T (or wavelength, but not both), height H, direction. For a wind sea: wind speed U, fetch F, duration t.

Fixed by the water, given T and depth h: wavelength from ω² = g·k·tanh(k·h); crest speed c = λ/T; group speed cg; orbits and velocities (which also depend on H).

Fetch-limited growth: Hs = 0.0016·√(gF/U²)·U²/g    Tp = 0.286·(gF/U²)⅓·U/g

Duration limit: gt/U = 68.8·(gF/U²)⅔    Fully developed: Hs ≈ 0.243·U²/g, Tp ≈ 8.1·U/g

Ship wake: c = V → λ = 2πV²/g, T = 2πV/g    Swell arrival time = distance ÷ (gT/4π)

6.5Where currents come from

A is the water itself moving. A wave is different: it is a shape passing through water that mostly stays in place (6.2). Currents carry vessels, debris and oil over long distances, and they push steadily, in one direction, on everything in the water: hulls, mooring lines, risers and pipelines.

Four things set the sea moving: the tide, the wind, the large-scale ocean circulation, and a handful of local effects. Each gives a different speed at different depths, so engineers describe a current as a : a speed and direction at each depth from the surface to the seabed.

1. Tides

reversing, predictable

The pull of the Moon and Sun raises the sea about twice a day. Water has to flow in and out to fill and empty every bay and shelf, so reverse roughly every six hours, with slack water in between. They are strongest where the flow is squeezed (straits, estuaries, shallow shelves) and can reach several knots. They are predictable years ahead and nearly uniform with depth, slowing only near the seabed.

2. Wind

thin surface layer

Wind dragging on the sea pushes the top layer along at about 2% of the wind speed (1.5 to 3%), so a 15 m/s gale gives roughly 0.6 kn. The effect fades with depth and design codes usually take it as gone by about 50 m. The Earth's rotation turns this to the right of the wind in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern.

3. Ocean circulation

steady streams and eddies

Global wind belts, the Earth's rotation and differences in water temperature and saltiness drive great : the Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Agulhas and East Australian Current. They run at 1 to 4 kn through the upper few hundred metres and shed that wander for weeks. Loop Current eddies in the Gulf of Mexico regularly halt drilling and installation work.

4. Local effects

site-specific

River outflow, and (wind and low pressure piling water against a coast). Below the surface, travel along the boundary between warm and cold layers and bring sudden current spikes lasting minutes, notably on Australia's North West Shelf and in the South China and Andaman Seas.

5. Drag grows with speed squared

u² law

The push of flowing water is : ½ × density × drag coefficient × area × speed². Double the current and the force is four times as large. A change from 1 kn to 2 kn sounds small but quadruples the load on a hull, line or riser.

6. Current reshapes the waves

wave–current interaction

Waves running against a current are slowed, so they bunch up: shorter, steeper and quicker to break. gives the notoriously short, steep seas of the Agulhas, Bass Strait and Pentland Firth. Waves running with a current are stretched and flattened.

Why it happens

Waves move water in near-closed orbits, so their main push reverses with every wave and largely cancels over each cycle. What is left is a much smaller steady force, plus as groups of bigger waves pass. A current moves water from one place to another, so its whole push is steady, and it is felt all the way down a riser or mooring line, not just near the surface where wave motion lives.

Flowing past a cylinder, water also sheds whirlpools alternately from each side, about 0.2 × speed ÷ diameter times a second. If that rate matches a natural frequency of a riser or a spar hull, it starts to vibrate across the flow: vortex-induced vibration or motion. Helical strakes on risers and spars break the whirlpools up.

Offshore decision: do ships account for currents?

Always. A tow plans its route, speed and departure around tide and current: a head current lengthens the voyage and the weather window needed; a cross-current makes the tow crab off its heading (8.3). Holding position, whether by tug, anchors or thrusters, has to resist wind, wave drift and current together. On a moored vessel current adds to the mean offset and line tension. Risers, mooring lines and pipelines are often governed by current: bending, VIV fatigue, clashing, and pipelines being rolled across the seabed. The basis therefore gives current profiles by direction and return period, and OrcaFlex and AQWA apply them alongside the wind and waves.

Misconception

"A knot of current is nothing next to a 4 m sea." The waves' main push is back and forth and mostly cancels; what remains is a smaller steady wave drift. The current pushes one way, all the time, and over the full water depth. In deep water the current is often the largest load on risers and mooring lines, and a strong eddy can stop an operation that the waves alone would allow.

Optional detail: profiles, drag and vortex shedding

Tidal: u(z) = utide,0·((d − z)/d)1/7    Wind-driven: u(z) = k·U10·(1 − z/d0) for z < d0, with k ≈ 0.015–0.03, d0 ≈ 50 m

Drag per metre on a cylinder: f = ½·ρ·Cd·D·u|u|    Waves and current together: use the combined velocity, (uwave + ucurrent)², not the two loads added (Morison's equation)

Vortex shedding frequency: fs ≈ 0.2·u/D    1 m/s past a 0.3 m riser: about 0.67 Hz

Because drag uses the combined velocity squared, a modest current on top of wave motion raises the peak load more than either alone would suggest: (1 + 1)² = 4 is double 1² + 1² = 2.

6.6Real seas are irregular

A real sea is many regular waves of different heights, periods and directions added together. No two waves are the same. Engineers summarise it with a and two numbers: the and a characteristic period such as the . Together they describe a , typically treated as steady over about three hours.

Why it happens

Hs is defined statistically (roughly the average of the highest third of waves, and close to what an observer would estimate by eye). Larger waves occur less often but they do occur, and the more waves you wait for, the bigger the largest one you are likely to see.

Offshore decision

Design and operational limits are usually stated in Hs and Tp, but structures, moorings and lifts must survive the largest individual wave or response expected in that sea state. Analyses therefore run long or many random simulations and use extreme-value statistics.

Misconception

"Hs = 3 m means waves are up to 3 m." Many waves are smaller, and some are much larger. In three hours of an Hs 3 m sea, a wave near 5.5 m is expected.

Easily confused terms: 13.4 One word, several statistics

6.7Wind, waves and current rarely line up

Wind changes in minutes. The wind sea follows it within hours. Swell arrives from storms far away, unrelated to the local wind. Currents come from tides, ocean circulation and local wind (6.5), and can turn with the tide. So a vessel can face wind from one side, swell from another and current from a third.

This is why a vessel does not simply point into the waves, and why engineers analyse many combinations of direction, not only the worst single direction for each load on its own.

6.8What a "100-year wave" means

Why it matters

A 100-year condition has a 1% chance of being exceeded in any given year. Over a 25-year field life, the chance of seeing it at least once is about 22%. Having just had one does not make the next one less likely.

Offshore decision

Permanent installations are typically designed for very rare conditions (return periods of 100 years and more, set by the governing standard). Short marine operations can be planned against a and a forecast instead, with margins for forecast uncertainty (Module 12).

Misconception

"We had the 100-year storm last year, so we're safe for a while." Each year's chance is independent. A return period is a probability, not a timetable.

Easily confused terms: 13.4 Return periods over a design life

6.9Where the wind, wave and current numbers come from

Every important shipping and towing route is mapped for wind, waves and current, but the maps answer different questions. A climate atlas says what a route is usually like in a given month. A tidal atlas says what the tide will do near the coast at any hour. A forecast says what it will actually be like this week. A gives the statistics an engineer designs to.

SourceExamplesWhat it givesUsed for
Climate atlasesPilot charts (US NGA Atlas of Pilot Charts); Admiralty Routeing Charts with Ocean Passages for the World (UK Hydrographic Office); Sailing DirectionsMonthly averages for each ocean: wind roses, prevailing current arrows and speeds, gale frequency, wave heights, ice limits, recommended routesChoosing a route and a season
Tidal dataTidal diamonds on nautical charts; tidal stream atlases for busy waters (English Channel, North Sea, Torres Strait)Hour-by-hour speed and direction of the tidal current, predictable years aheadTiming departures, arrivals and passages through straits
Forecasts and ocean modelsECMWF and NOAA GFS (wind), WAVEWATCH III (waves), Copernicus Marine, HYCOM and NOAA RTOFS (currents); viewers such as Windy and earth.nullschool.netThe actual conditions for the next days, including where eddies and current cores are today and go/no-go decisions in a
Hindcasts and wave statisticsERA5, Oceanweather GROW, BMT Global Wave Statistics; site studies and current-meter measurementsDecades of past weather rebuilt on a grid, turned into extremes by area, season, direction and Design conditions for tows, moorings and fixed installations: the basis

Why there are four kinds

Weather is a mix of a predictable part (the season, the tide) and a chaotic part (the storm or eddy that happens to be there). Atlases and tidal tables capture the predictable part; forecasts capture the chaotic part, but only a week or so ahead. A design has to cover weather nobody can forecast yet, so it relies on statistics from long hindcasts.

Offshore decision

An unrestricted tow, too long to rely on a forecast, is designed for the extremes that the route and season can produce, taken from wave statistics for each ocean area it crosses. A operation, short enough to sail on a reliable forecast, uses forecast limits instead, with margins for forecast error. Major tows and heavy-lift voyages almost always also employ a weather routing service, which updates the track and timing as forecasts change.

Misconception

"The pilot chart shows 1 knot, so plan for 1 knot." Atlases show averages over many years. On the day, the current inside an eddy or a shifted Gulf Stream core can be three or four times that, and in straits and off headlands the tide can exceed anything an ocean-scale map shows. Open-ocean maps are coarse; coastal passages need local tidal data and fixed sites need their own measurements.

Watch How science explains monster waves (Physics Girl) · Rogue Waves Can Be Four Times Larger Than We Thought (Bright Side) · more videos

What you should now understand

  • Waves have height, period, wavelength and direction. Period controls wavelength and speed.
  • Water particles move in orbits that shrink quickly with depth; the wave shape travels, the water mostly does not.
  • The source sets period, height and direction; the water then fixes wavelength and speed. For a wind sea, wind speed, fetch and duration set Hs and Tp.
  • Real seas are irregular. Hs and Tp summarise a sea state; individual waves can be nearly twice Hs.
  • Currents come from tides, wind, ocean circulation and local effects. They vary with depth, push steadily one way, and their drag grows with speed squared.
  • Wind, wind sea, swell and current can all act from different directions.
  • Climate atlases, tidal data, forecasts and hindcasts each answer a different question; design uses hindcast statistics, operations use forecasts.
  • A return period is an annual probability, not a schedule.
In practice

Analyses start from a basis: tables of Hs, Tp, wind and current by direction and return period, often supplied by the client or a metocean specialist. AQWA and OrcaFlex then run the vessel or system through many of these conditions. Choosing which combinations to run is an engineering judgement in itself.

Module 7 · Seakeeping

Six degrees of freedom and seakeeping

A floating body can move in six independent ways. How much it moves depends less on how big the waves are than on whether their rhythm matches the vessel's own natural rhythm.

The question

Two vessels sit side by side in the same 2 m swell. One barely moves; the other rolls so much that crane work has to stop. Why?

7.1Three translations, three rotations

Surge · Sway · Heave

translations, metres

is fore-and-aft along x, is sideways along y, is up and down along z.

Roll · Pitch · Yaw

rotations, degrees

tilts side to side about x, tilts bow up and down about y, turns the heading about z.

Which ones have springs?

restoring forces

Heave, roll and pitch have hydrostatic restoring forces (buoyancy pushes back), so they have natural periods. Surge, sway and yaw have none: only moorings, thrusters or towlines hold them.

Easily confused terms: 13.2 The steady counterpart of each motion

7.2Natural period and resonance

Push a floating vessel down and let go, and it bobs at its own , set by its mass (including water that moves with it) and its hydrostatic stiffness. If waves arrive with a period close to that, each wave adds to the motion before the last one has died away: . Only limits it.

Why it happens

Long waves (far right of the curve) are slow and gentle: the vessel simply follows the water surface, so the heave RAO tends to 1 m per m.

Near the natural period, wave pushes arrive in step with the vessel's own oscillation and build it up.

Short waves push some parts of the hull up while others go down, so the forces largely cancel, and the vessel's inertia resists quick changes.

Offshore decision

Designers choose hull shape and mass distribution to put natural periods away from the energetic wave periods at the site. Semi-submersibles, for example, have small waterplanes and long heave periods, well above most wave periods. Operations are planned for headings and seasons that avoid resonance.

Misconceptions

  • "Bigger waves always mean bigger motions." Period matters as much as height.
  • "If the vessel is strong enough, the operation is fine." A vessel can be structurally safe while moving far too much for a crane lift, a gangway transfer or a diver.
Optional detail: the oscillator and the response spectrum

(M + A) ẍ + B ẋ + C x = F(t)    natural period Tn = 2π √((M + A) / C)

M is mass, A is , B is damping and C is hydrostatic stiffness (ρ g Awp for heave, Δ g GM for roll). The dynamic amplification at frequency ratio r = ω/ωn and damping ratio ζ is 1 / √((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²).

In an irregular sea, the response spectrum is the wave spectrum multiplied by the RAO squared: Sresponse(ω) = |RAO(ω)|² · Swave(ω). That is the shaded curve in the lower chart. Significant response comes from its area, the same way Hs comes from the wave spectrum.

Period and frequency

two ways to say the same thing

The is the time for one complete cycle, in seconds. The frequency is how many cycles happen per second (hertz). Angular frequency counts the same thing as an angle swept per second, with one cycle being 2π radians (radians per second, used in RAO plots). A 10 s period is a frequency of 0.1 Hz. Long period = low frequency.

A child on a swing

resonance, everyday

Push a swing at random moments and little happens. Push once per swing, in time with its own rhythm, and small pushes build a big motion. Waves do the same to a vessel whose natural period matches theirs. Push at the wrong rhythm and the swing barely moves, however hard you push.

Shock absorbers

damping, everyday

A car without shock absorbers keeps bouncing after a bump; damping takes the energy out. In water, the waves a hull makes as it moves and the eddies shed by bilge keels play that role. Low damping is why roll can grow so large at resonance.

7.3Added mass and damping, seen in the water

An is a vessel's motion "transfer function": for each wave period (or frequency) and direction, how much motion per unit of wave. Translational RAOs (surge, sway, heave) are in metres per metre of wave amplitude. Rotational RAOs (roll, pitch, yaw) are in degrees per metre, or sometimes normalised by wave slope. Each RAO also has a , which says when the peak motion happens relative to the wave crest.

7.4From motion to force: why cargo needs seafastening

Motions matter to structures because moving things need forces to move them. When a barge rolls, its deck cargo is tilted and swung from side to side. At the end of each roll two effects push the cargo sideways: part of its weight now acts along the tilted deck, and the hull is braking to a stop and reversing, so the cargo tries to keep going, like a standing passenger thrown forward when a bus brakes hard. The (welded brackets, stoppers and chains) must hold both.

Why it happens

Force = mass × acceleration. Roll motion is fastest through upright and slows to a stop at each extreme, where it reverses. The acceleration at the extreme grows with the square of how quickly the vessel rolls (shorter period, much bigger) and in proportion to the distance from the roll axis (taller, bigger).

Offshore decision

Transport engineers take the motions from Module 7 analysis (or code defaults), turn them into accelerations at each cargo item, and design seafastening, grillage and deck strength for the resulting forces (Module 10). They may choose a heading, season or ballast condition that softens the roll, because a gentler roll means lighter, cheaper seafastening.

Misconception

"A heavy module will stay put under its own weight." Friction cannot be relied on at sea: deck wetness, vibration and vertical accelerations reduce it just when it is needed. Seafastening is designed to carry the full sideways load.

Watch Ship Motions Explained: Roll, Pitch, Yaw, Surge, Sway, and Heave (Nautical Academy) · Why Boats Move the Way They Do (6 Degrees of Freedom) (Offshore Surveys) · more videos

What you should now understand

  • Six degrees of freedom: surge, sway, heave (translations, metres); roll, pitch, yaw (rotations, degrees).
  • Heave, roll and pitch have natural periods. Waves near those periods cause resonance, limited by damping.
  • Added mass is water that moves with the hull; radiation damping is energy carried off by the waves the hull makes.
  • An RAO gives response per unit wave for each period and direction. Combined with a wave spectrum, it predicts motion in an irregular sea.
  • Motion limits for operations are separate from structural strength.
  • Motions become forces: tilt plus acceleration at the extreme of each roll push deck cargo sideways, and seafastening must hold it.
In practice

This is the heart of and work. AQWA computes RAOs, added mass and damping for a hull; those feed OrcaFlex, which simulates the vessel with its moorings, risers, towlines or crane loads through time. Results are compared against motion criteria for each operation and used to derive accelerations for seafastening design (Module 10).

Module 8 · Resistance and towing

Resistance, propulsion, towing and squat

Moving a hull through water costs force, and the cost rises steeply with speed. For an unpowered barge, that force comes through a towline from a tug, and the towline becomes a structural component in its own right.

The question

A tug has 100 tonnes of bollard pull. The loaded barge needs only about 15 tonnes of pull to make 5 knots in calm water. Is the tow safe?

8.1Where the resistance comes from

Frictional resistance

skin friction

Water sticks to the hull and is dragged along in a thin boundary layer. Grows with wetted area and roughly with speed squared. Dominant for long, slender hulls at low speed. Marine growth and rough paint increase it.

Form (pressure) drag

shape, eddies

A blunt shape leaves a wake of eddies, and the pressure behind it never fully recovers. Small for streamlined ships, large for square-ended barges. A raked bow on a barge reduces it.

Wave-making resistance

energy into waves

A moving hull makes waves, and the energy in them comes from the thrust. Rises very steeply as the wave the hull makes approaches the hull's own length (a effect).

Added resistance and environment

waves, wind, current

Waves add resistance by reflecting off and moving the hull. Wind pushes on everything above water, including tall cargo. Current changes the speed through the water.

8.2Towing experiment

Why it happens

Resistance depends on , not over the ground. A 2-knot head current means the tug must push the barge through the water at 7 knots to make 5 knots of , which needs much more force.

A long, heavy towline hangs in a . The sag acts as a shock absorber: as the barge surges in waves, the line straightens and slackens instead of jerking. Pull harder or shorten the line, and the sag disappears, so wave-induced grow.

Offshore decision

Tow planning checks that the tug can hold the tow against a defined severe weather condition (not just make speed in calm water), sizes the towline and connections for peak dynamic loads, sets the towline length, and plans the route, weather limits, ports of refuge and emergency gear. guidelines such as DNV-ST-N001 set the criteria.

Misconception

"Enough bollard pull means the tow is safe." is measured at zero speed in calm water. In a storm the tug's effective thrust falls, the barge's resistance rises, the towline sees large peak loads, and the barge's own stability, motions and seafastening all have to hold.

8.3Speed through water versus speed over ground

The water itself moves. A cross-current pushes the tow sideways, so to follow a planned track the tow must point partly into the current (), which also changes the angle the waves and wind hit it at. Wind adds its own sideways drift through the water, called ; a barge with tall cargo can make a knot or more of leeway in a strong beam wind.

So the direction the bow points (the ) and the direction the vessel actually travels over the seabed (its , or ) are often different. Navigation displays show both. Watch the abbreviation: on a chart plotter COG means course over ground, while in a stability report CoG means centre of gravity.

Easily confused terms: 13.5 Where it is measured from

8.4Propulsion losses: from engine to towline

8.5Shallow water: squat, the pull towards the seabed

A vessel moving through shallow water sits lower than it does at rest, and usually trims too. This sinkage is called , and it is one of the main causes of groundings in ports and channels. It happens even though nothing has been loaded and the hull has not changed.

Why it happens

As the hull moves, water must flow back past it to fill the space it leaves behind. In shallow water the only route is the narrow gap under the keel and along the sides, so the water there speeds up. Faster flow means lower pressure (Bernoulli's principle), so the water surface around the hull drops and the hull drops with it. Less pressure underneath also means the seabed seems to "pull" the hull down.

The pressure drop grows with speed squared, which is why squat roughly quadruples when speed doubles. A full-bodied hull (high block coefficient) usually squats by the bow; a fine-lined one by the stern.

Offshore decision

Tow routes out of fabrication yards often cross shallow channels and bars. The plan sets a minimum that must allow for squat, tide, wave-induced heave, pitch and roll, and survey uncertainty. It also sets a maximum speed for the shallow section and the tidal window in which it can be crossed. A towed barge on a long line also feels near channel sides.

Misconception

"If the draft is less than the charted depth, the vessel is safe." The draft is measured at rest. Underway in shallow water the vessel can sit half a metre to over a metre deeper, more when it rolls or pitches in a swell. Several large ships have grounded in channels that were deeper than their static draft.

Squat (hydrodynamic)

needs motion through water

Caused by flow speeding up under a moving hull. It disappears when the vessel stops. Controlled by speed, depth and the hull's fullness.

Bank effect (hydrodynamic)

near a channel side

The same low pressure, but between the hull and a nearby bank. The stern is sucked towards the bank and the bow pushed away, which can swing the vessel across the channel.

Seabed breakout suction (soil)

needs contact with soft seabed

A different effect with a similar name. An object resting on soft clay, or a barge grounded on mud, is held down because water cannot flow in under it quickly when it is lifted. The extra force to free it, the , can be a large fraction of its weight and is checked in subsea lift plans.

Easily confused terms: 13.2 Draft, sinkage, squat and heave

Watch The Squat Effect or Shallow Water Effect (marineBuddies) · Understanding Shallow Water Effects on Ships: how Bernoulli’s principle influences ship behaviour (Sailor’s Compass) · more videos

What you should now understand

  • Resistance comes from friction, form drag and wave-making, plus wind, waves and current. It rises steeply with speed.
  • Resistance depends on speed through the water. Currents change the speed over ground and the track.
  • A towline's catenary sag absorbs shock; tight lines see high snatch loads in waves.
  • In shallow water a moving vessel squats: it sinks and trims because the flow under it speeds up. Squat grows roughly with speed squared and eats into under-keel clearance.
  • Bollard pull is a calm-water, zero-speed rating. Tow safety also depends on holding capacity in bad weather, towline strength, stability, motions and planning.
In practice

engineering combines everything so far: stability of the loaded barge, its motions on the route, required bollard pull, towline and bridle design, and the forces on the cargo's seafastening. OrcaFlex can model the tug–towline–barge system dynamically to find peak towline tensions in waves.

Module 9 · Hull form

Hull, bow and stern shapes, and the parts that steer and steady them

A hull's shape decides how much it can carry, how hard it is to push, how it moves in waves and how it steers. This module lets you turn hulls, bows, sterns and their fittings around in 3D and look at them along each axis, the way naval architects draw them.

The question

A transport barge, a bulk carrier and a container ship can all be about as wide as each other. Why do they look so different under the water, and what does each shape buy?

9.1Reading a hull in three views

A hull is a curved 3D surface, so naval architects describe it with three flat views, one along each axis. Together they make the : the profile (side view, x against z), the half-breadth plan (top view, x against y, with curves called waterlines at several heights) and the body plan (end view, y against z, with cross-sections called ). Drag the model below and use the view buttons to line it up with each axis; the lines plan underneath shows the same hull in all three views at once.

Block coefficient Cb

volume ÷ (L × B × T)

How much of the enclosing box the underwater hull fills. A box barge is 1.0, a bulk carrier about 0.85, a container ship about 0.6, a tug about 0.55. Fuller means more displacement for the same dimensions, but more resistance at speed.
