Midship coefficient Cm

midship section area ÷ (B × T)

How square the biggest cross-section is. Most ships are 0.95 to 0.99: flat bottom, vertical sides and a small rounded bilge. Fast, fine boats have V-shaped sections and lower values.

Prismatic coefficient Cp

volume ÷ (midship area × L)

How the volume is spread along the length: high means the ends are full, low means the volume is concentrated amidships. It is the coefficient most closely linked to wave-making resistance. Cb = Cp × Cm.

Waterplane coefficient Cwp

waterplane area ÷ (L × B)

How full the waterline is, seen from above. It sets how much the vessel sinks per tonne added and, with the beam, how stiff it is in roll (Modules 3 and 4).

Parallel midbody

the straight middle

The length over which the cross-section does not change. Full cargo ships have a long one, which is cheap to build (identical blocks) and easy to berth. Its ends are the (bow) and the run (stern).

Proportions

L/B and B/T

Long and slender (high L/B) makes less wave resistance; wide and shallow (high B/T) gives roll stiffness and deck area but a lively roll. Barges are short and wide (L/B about 3), container ships long and slender (about 6 to 7).

Bilge radius and flare

section shape

The rounds the corner between bottom and side; a sharp corner (as on barges) damps roll more but costs some resistance. is the outward spread of the bow sections above the waterline, which throws spray aside and adds buoyancy as the bow dips.

Easily confused terms: 13.2 Draft, trim and the other steady quantities

9.2Bow shapes

The bow decides how the hull meets the water and the waves: how much wave it makes, how it rides over a swell and whether it slams. The six common shapes below are all fitted to the same 100 m hull. Drag any panel to turn all six together.

BowShapeWhat it doesWhere you meet it
Square (box)Flat vertical endCheapest possible; pushes a wall of water, so very high resistance and slammingPontoons, dumb barges in sheltered water
Flat plate sloping up from the bottom to a short Lets water flow under the hull; removes much of the square bow's drag using flat plates only, and keeps full deck widthTransport and cargo barges
Vertical stemUpright stem, fine waterlinesLongest waterline for a given overall length (good for speed and capacity); wetter in wavesMany modern cargo ships and ferries
Stem leaning forward going up, often with Bow rises over waves instead of burying; flare adds buoyancy and throws spray asideTugs, older ships, many offshore vessels
A rounded bulb below the waterlineMakes its own wave that partly cancels the bow wave, cutting resistance by several per cent at the design speed and draft; can add resistance at other speeds or in ballastLarge cargo ships, tankers, FPSO conversions
Foremost point near the waterline, stem leaning back above it, high enclosed bowPierces waves rather than riding up and slamming down: less pitching, less slamming and less speed loss in head seasOffshore supply and construction vessels

9.3Stern shapes

The stern has to let the water close in smoothly behind the hull, feed the propeller with an even flow and leave room for the rudder. A stern that ends too abruptly under water drags a turbulent wake behind it; one that is too fine has no room for machinery or deck space.

flat, wide end

Simple to build and gives a wide, square working deck aft, which offshore vessels need for cranes, A-frames and cargo. At speed the water breaks cleanly off the transom edge. In following seas a wide transom can slam.

rounded, overhanging

The hull curves in to a rounded end above the water. Good flow to the propeller and gentle in following seas, but less deck area. Common on tugs and older ships.

Raked barge stern and skegs

flat plate, fins below

A flat rake like the bow's, usually with two underneath. The skegs keep a towed barge tracking straight instead of swinging behind the tug.

Twin-skeg sterns

two propellers, two fins

Larger ships and offshore vessels with two propellers often have two skeg-shaped "legs" at the stern, each housing a shaft. They give clean flow to each propeller and good course stability.

9.4Rudders, propellers, ducts, thrusters, fins and keels

Beyond the main hull, a set of smaller parts, called , does much of the work of driving, steering and steadying a vessel. They are small compared with the hull but change its behaviour a great deal, and they also add drag. Choose a propulsion arrangement and the extras below, then pick a part to highlight it and read what it does.

PartWhat it changesTrade-off
and Steering: side force at the sternNeeds water flowing over it; a flap rudder gives more force but is more complex
: fixed or Thrust; a controllable-pitch propeller changes blade angle instead of shaft speed, giving fine control and quick reversalEfficiency against cost and complexity; cavitation and vibration
More thrust at low speed and high load: higher bollard pullExtra drag at high speed; can clog or be damaged in ice
Thrust in any direction; no rudder; precise manoeuvring and DPCost, mechanical complexity; vulnerable to grounding
Sideways push at the bow (or stern) at low speedUseless above a few knots; tunnel openings add drag
Straight-line stability; protect the propellerMake the vessel harder to turn
Roll damping: smaller roll near resonanceSmall drag; nothing else, which is why almost every ship has them
Active roll reduction, very effective at speedCost and maintenance; most need forward speed
Water sloshing between side tanks, timed to oppose roll; works at zero speed (useful for DP and crane vessels)Takes space and weight, and its free surface reduces GM
Lift the stern at speed: less trim and less resistanceLittle effect at low speed
Energy-saving devicesDucts and fins just ahead of the propeller that straighten and pre-swirl the flow, saving a few per cent of fuelEach gain is small and depends on the hull

Why small parts matter

Steering and roll damping both come from forces that are small compared with the hull's weight but act far from its centre. A rudder 40 m behind the centre of gravity turns a 9,000 t vessel with a side force well under 1% of its weight. A bilge keel only half a metre wide sheds eddies all along the hull each time it rolls, taking energy out of the motion.

Offshore decision

The propulsion arrangement sets what a vessel can do: azimuth thrusters and tunnel thrusters make dynamic positioning possible; ducted propellers set a tug's bollard pull; stabilisers and anti-roll tanks widen the weather window for crane and walk-to-work operations. Motion analyses must include appendage damping, especially bilge keels, or roll is badly over-predicted.

Misconception

"Bilge keels make a vessel more stable." They do not change GM or the GZ curve at all. They damp roll, so the vessel rolls less in waves, especially near resonance. Stability and damping are separate: a vessel can be very stable and still roll badly if it is lightly damped.

9.5Offshore hull forms: why platforms are shaped so differently

A floating platform that has to stay put for 20 years in one place cares less about resistance and more about motions. The key number is the compared with the displaced volume. The waterplane provides the "spring" in heave (Module 7), so a hull with a small waterplane and a big volume has a long heave natural period, well above the periods of most waves.

Barge and ship-shaped

large waterplane

Lots of deck area and storage, cheap to build or convert. But the large waterplane makes them follow the waves: heave and roll periods sit near ordinary wave periods. FPSOs use a turret so they can weathervane and take the waves on the bow.

small waterplane

Buoyancy sits in pontoons well below the surface, where wave action is weaker, and only slender columns cross the waterline. Gentle motions for drilling, crane work and accommodation. Ballasting changes the draft between transit and operation.

tiny waterplane, deep draft

One very deep cylinder. Its heave period is far above the wave periods, and its centre of buoyancy is high above a deep, heavy keel, making it very stable. The deep hull can suffer vortex-induced motion in strong currents, so spars often have helical strakes.

Tension-leg platform

held down by tendons

A semi-submersible-like hull pulled down by vertical steel tendons anchored to the seabed. The tendons almost remove heave, pitch and roll altogether, which allows wellheads on deck. Not shown in the model.

Watch Why Don't Cruise Ships Tip Over? (Casual Navigation) · Casual Navigation channel · more videos

What you should now understand

  • A hull is described by three views along its axes: profile, half-breadth plan and body plan, together the lines plan.
  • Form coefficients summarise the shape: Cb for overall fullness, Cm for the midship section, Cp for how volume is spread along the length, Cwp for the waterline.
  • Full hulls carry more for their size; fine hulls make less wave resistance at speed. Barges trade both for cheapness and deck area.
  • Bows set wave-making and behaviour in head seas: raked barge bows, raked and vertical stems, bulbous bows and inverted X-bows each solve a different problem.
  • Sterns feed the propeller and carry the rudder; transoms give deck area, cruiser sterns gentler flow, skegs straight-line stability.
  • Appendages steer (rudders, thrusters), drive (propellers, ducts) and steady (bilge keels, fins, tanks) the vessel. Bilge keels damp roll; they do not add stability.
  • Offshore floaters with a small waterplane for their volume (semi-submersibles, spars) have long heave periods and move gently in waves.
In practice

Hull form arrives in an offshore project as data: a lines plan or 3D surface model, hydrostatic tables and a stability booklet. The same geometry is meshed into panels for to compute wave loads and RAOs, while appendage effects such as bilge-keel roll damping are added on top, because panel methods do not capture them on their own.

Module 10 · Structures

Structural strength and FEA intuition

Weight and buoyancy balance overall, but not at every point along the hull. The mismatch bends the whole vessel like a beam, while local loads press on individual plates and brackets. Structural analysis asks whether the steel can carry both, once and millions of times.

The question

A barge carrying a heavy module in its middle meets a wave as long as itself. Where is the steel most stressed, and does it matter whether the crest or the trough is amidships?

10.1The hull as a floating beam

Why it happens

At each point along the hull, the local weight and local buoyancy differ. The net load (up where buoyancy wins, down where weight wins) produces and along the hull, just like loads on a bridge girder. The bending moment is largest near the middle; the shear force is largest about a quarter of the way in from each end.

Offshore decision

Before a transport, engineers check the barge's (hull bending and shear) for the loading condition and route waves, and its under the cargo's support points. They may move cargo or adjust ballast to reduce the still-water bending moment.

Misconception

"If it floats level, the hull isn't loaded." A barge can float perfectly level with a large internal bending moment, because the weight is concentrated where buoyancy is spread out.

Easily confused terms: 13.3 Still-water versus wave bending moment

10.2Stress, deformation and the four basic actions

Tension

pulled apart

Fibres lengthen. A mooring chain, a towline, the deck of a hogging hull.

Compression

pushed together

Fibres shorten. Jacket legs, the deck of a sagging hull. Slender members in compression can buckle.

Bending

tension one side, compression the other

A beam curves; one face stretches, the other squeezes, and the middle (neutral axis) does neither.

Shear

layers sliding

Adjacent sections try to slide past each other. Carried mostly by webs and side .

is force per unit area inside the material (megapascals, MPa). is how far things move. They are related but not the same: a long, thin member can deflect a lot at low stress, and a short, stiff one can be highly stressed while barely moving. Strength checks limit stress; serviceability checks limit deformation.

How big is a megapascal?

1 MPa = 1 newton per square millimetre

Typical offshore steel (grade S355) starts to yield at about 355 MPa: each square millimetre can carry about 36 kg. A bar 1 cm² in cross-section therefore holds about 3.6 tonnes before it starts to stretch permanently. Design allows only a fraction of that, through safety factors.

Stress and strain

load and stretch

Stress is load per area; strain is stretch per length. Steel stretches in proportion to stress (it springs back) up to yield. Its stiffness, Young's modulus, is about 210,000 MPa: at yield, steel has stretched only about 0.17%.

10.3Three different ways steel fails

Why repeated moderate loads matter

Every wave flexes the structure a little. A crack-like flaw at a weld toe grows a tiny amount with each cycle. Over 20 years an offshore structure sees on the order of 100 million wave cycles. Fatigue life is very sensitive to stress range: in the common S–N model, halving the stress range gives about eight times the life.

Offshore decision

Fatigue often governs design for long-term moored units, risers and mooring components, while extreme loads govern for short tows. Detail design (smooth transitions, weld quality, avoiding stress concentrations) can matter as much as plate thickness.

Misconception

"If stresses are below yield, the structure is fine." Below-yield stresses can still cause buckling (if compressive and slender) and fatigue (if repeated). Each failure mode has its own check.

10.4What finite element analysis does

splits a structure into many small whose behaviour is simple, links them at nodes, applies loads and , and solves for how every node moves. Stresses follow from the displacements. Strand7 and ANSYS do this with thousands to millions of elements; the bracket below uses up to a few thousand, solved live in your browser.

What can go wrong

  • Boundary conditions: too few supports and the model can float away (no solution); too many and it is unrealistically stiff.
  • Mesh quality: coarse meshes under-predict stress gradients; sharp re-entrant corners produce stresses that grow without limit as the mesh is refined.
  • Interpretation: results must be read at the right location, in the right stress measure, against the right criterion.

Offshore decision

FEA is used for seafastening, grillages, lift points, padeyes, spreader bars and local hull strength under concentrated cargo loads. Engineers check reactions against applied loads, look at the deformed shape for sense, refine meshes where it matters and use code-defined hot-spot or nominal stress methods rather than raw peak values.

Misconception

"The model ran and the plot is mostly blue, so it's fine." A plot only shows what the model was told. Wrong loads, supports or units produce confident, colourful, wrong answers.

Watch Why Are Big Ships Bendy? (Casual Navigation) · Forces experienced by a ship: shearing force, bending moments, hogging and sagging (Steering Mariners) · Understanding the Finite Element Method (The Efficient Engineer) · more videos

What you should now understand

  • Uneven weight and buoyancy bend the hull: crest amidships hogs it, trough amidships sags it.
  • Global strength is the whole hull as a beam; local strength is plates and frames under specific loads.
  • Stress is internal force per area; deformation is movement. Deeper sections cut stress and deflection sharply.
  • Yielding, buckling and fatigue are separate failure modes with separate checks.
  • FEA results depend on boundary conditions, mesh and interpretation. Exaggerated plots are for insight, not proof.
In practice

in Strand7 or ANSYS takes loads from the earlier modules: weights and centres of gravity, accelerations from vessel motions, towline and mooring tensions, lift loads with dynamic factors. It checks members and connections against code criteria (for example in DNV, API or AISC standards) for yielding, buckling and fatigue.

Module 11 · Systems

Offshore systems: connecting the foundations

A floating installation is a system: a hull held by moorings, connected to the seabed by risers, fed by flowlines, and put there by installation vessels. Each part feels the motions of the others.

The question

A storm pushes a moored production vessel 40 m off its station. What happens to the mooring lines, the anchors and the flexible riser carrying oil up from the seabed?

11.1The parts of a floating installation

11.2Offset, mooring tension and the riser

Why it happens

A catenary mooring holds the vessel mainly by the weight of chain it lifts off the seabed. Small offsets lift a little more chain: a soft spring. As the offset grows, the line approaches a straight line from anchor to fairlead and becomes very stiff, so tension rises steeply.

The riser hangs from the same vessel, so every metre of offset changes its shape: stretched on one side, slack and compressed on the other.

Offshore decision

Mooring design balances offset (which the risers can only tolerate within limits) against line tension (which the chain, connectors and anchors must survive with margins). Engineers also check the case with one line broken, because the remaining lines must still hold.

Misconception

"Mooring lines are like ropes pulling tight." A catenary line works mostly by its weight and shape. Most of its length is often lying on the seabed, and it is designed to keep some of it there so the anchor is pulled horizontally.

Easily confused terms: 13.2 Mean offset, slow drift and wave-frequency motion

11.3Five things that connect a vessel to the world

ElementJobMain loadsTypical analysis
Keep a vessel on station for months or yearsMean environment, slow drift, wave-frequency motion; line failure casesCoupled dynamic simulation (OrcaFlex), anchor capacity (geotechnical)
Pull an unpowered barge or structure from A to BTow resistance, wind, snatch loads in wavesBollard pull and towline checks, dynamic tow simulation
Carry fluids between seabed and a moving vesselVessel motions, current, waves, internal pressure, self-weightDynamic analysis of shape, tension, curvature and fatigue (OrcaFlex)
Carry fluids along the seabed between wells, manifolds and riser basesPressure, temperature expansion, on-bottom stability in currents, installation loadsMostly static and thermal expansion analysis; installation analysis while laying
Hold position with computer-controlled thrusters instead of linesMean environment and drift forces, matched by thrustDP capability plots: which weather the thrusters can hold, including after a failure

Static equilibrium vs dynamic response

analysis finds where forces balance under steady loads: the mean offset and mean tension. analysis follows motions through time, capturing inertia, damping and peaks. Moorings and risers usually need both: a static case to set up, then dynamic simulations for extremes and fatigue.

Global vs local analysis

analysis models the whole system coarsely (vessel, all lines, risers) to get motions and line loads. analysis takes those loads into a detailed model of one part, such as a fairlead, padeye or riser hang-off, to check stresses. Global results are the inputs to local checks.

Easily confused terms: 13.7 Names that depend on the job

Watch How does an FPSO work? (Piping Technology) · APL Turret Mooring Systems (Offshore, Maritime and Energy) · Stones FPSO Turret Mooring System (SBM Offshore) · more videos

What you should now understand

  • Moorings, anchors, risers, flowlines and installation vessels form one interacting system.
  • Catenary moorings stiffen as offset grows; tension rises faster than offset.
  • Drag anchors want horizontal pull; seabed soil governs which anchor works and how much it can hold.
  • Risers move with the vessel and need dynamic analysis; flowlines on the seabed are mostly static once installed.
  • Global analysis provides loads; local analysis checks details.
In practice

Mooring and , flowline design, installation engineering and assessment map directly onto this picture. A typical chain: AQWA for vessel hydrodynamics, OrcaFlex for the coupled mooring and riser dynamics, geotechnical assessment of anchor or foundation capacity in the site soils, and Strand7 or ANSYS for local structural checks.

Module 12 · Judgement

Design trade-offs and engineering judgement

Almost every improvement costs something somewhere else. Engineering judgement is knowing which costs matter for this operation, and showing with analysis that the chosen balance meets agreed criteria.

The question

The client wants to mount a heavier crane higher on the vessel to reach further. Why can't the engineers just say yes?

12.1Trade-off explorer

12.2Choosing a weather window

Why it matters

An operation that must not be interrupted halfway (a heavy lift, a float-over, a tow out of shelter) needs a continuous spell of good weather longer than its duration plus contingency. Forecasts are uncertain, so the limit used for go/no-go decisions is lower than the limit the equipment can actually tolerate.

Offshore decision

Engineers choose the season, design the operation to tolerate a higher Hs where it is economic (stronger rigging, better vessel), shorten durations, and plan safe hold points where the operation can pause.

Misconception

"If the crane can work in 2.5 m seas, we go whenever the forecast says 2.5 m." The go limit is lower than the physical limit, because the forecast can be wrong and the weather must stay good for the whole operation.

12.3Standards: API, DNV and ABS

API

American Petroleum Institute

Industry standards and recommended practices widely used for offshore structures, stationkeeping, risers and subsea equipment, for example API RP 2A for fixed platforms and API RP 2SK for stationkeeping systems.

DNV

classification society and standards body

Publishes offshore standards and recommended practices (for example on environmental loads, fatigue, position mooring and marine operations) and classes ships and offshore units. Its DNV-ST-N001 is widely used for marine operations and marine warranty.

ABS

American Bureau of Shipping

A . Its rules and guides define how vessels and offshore units must be designed, built and maintained to receive and keep "class", with surveys through their life.

Who checks what

roles

Class societies certify the vessel or unit. A reviews and approves specific marine operations on behalf of insurers. Flag and coastal-state regulators set legal requirements. The engineering contractor does the analysis and is responsible for it.

Three different things are often blurred together:

1. Physical analysis

What will happen? Motions, tensions, stresses, offsets, from models such as AQWA, OrcaFlex or Strand7.

e.g. max line tension in the 100-year storm

2. Design criteria

What is acceptable? Allowable stresses, safety or load factors, motion limits, from standards, equipment makers and the project.

e.g. tension must not exceed breaking strength ÷ the required safety factor

3. Acceptance check

Compare demand with capacity for every relevant case. Report utilisation, usually as a ratio that must not exceed 1.0.

e.g. utilisation = factored demand ÷ capacity

4. Review and approval

Independent checking, class approval or marine warranty approval of the operation, with conditions such as weather limits.

e.g. certificate of approval for the tow

Note. This guide quotes no acceptance limits to design against. The few factors it mentions, such as a DAF of 1.2 or the 1.67 mooring factor in 13.3, are examples only: real values depend on the standard, its edition, the consequence class and the project. Its simulations illustrate physics; they cannot approve any real design or operation.

What you should now understand

  • Raising weight improves motion comfort and reach but costs stability. Thicker steel cuts stress but adds weight and cost. Stiffer moorings cut offset but raise dynamic tension.
  • Weather windows depend on operation duration, the physical limit and forecast uncertainty; longer and less tolerant operations find fewer windows.
  • Analysis predicts behaviour; criteria define acceptable; checks compare them; reviewers approve.
  • API, DNV and ABS publish the standards and rules that define most criteria offshore.
In practice

A large part of the value is in this judgement: choosing which cases to analyse, which standard governs, where margins are thin and how to make an operation more robust. When you read an engineering report, look for the chain: inputs and assumptions, analysis results, the criteria used, the utilisation, and any conditions on the approval.

Module 13 · Vocabulary

Terms that get confused

Offshore engineering often has two or three words for what looks like one thing: heel, list and roll; trim and pitch; offset and drift. The differences are deliberate. Each word says what causes the effect, whether it is steady or oscillating, and which number it should be checked against. This module groups those words into families and shows what separates them.

The question

A report says the barge "heels 8° and rolls 5°". A colleague reads that as 13°; another as 5°. Who is right, and why does the report use two words?

13.1Steady versus oscillating: heel, list, loll and roll

All four words describe the vessel tilting sideways about its long axis. They differ in two ways: what causes the tilt (weight inside the vessel, or a force from outside) and whether it stays put or swings. The same two questions sort almost every family in this module.

TermCaused byBehaviourGoes away whenChecked against
Weight inside the vessel off the centreline: cargo, ballast, fuel, a flooded compartmentSteady tilt, even in calm waterWeight is moved or ballast is pumpedOperating limits for cargo, cranes and deck equipment
A steady outside force: wind on the side, a crane load swung outboard, a towline pulling sideways, turningSteady tilt while the force actsThe force stopsStability criteria: the heeling lever against the GZ curve
Negative GM: the vessel is unstable uprightRests at an angle to one side, and can flop to the otherG is lowered (weight down low, or removed up high)A warning sign, never an acceptable condition
WavesOscillation back and forth around the resting angleThe waves stopMotion criteria, seafastening forces, downflooding angle at the extreme

Why it happens

A floating vessel always tries to rest where the righting lever balances whatever is tipping it. Off-centre weight moves G sideways, so the balance point moves: that is list. A steady wind adds a heeling lever, so the balance point moves further: that is heel. Neither needs anything to move once it has settled.

Waves push the vessel away from that balance point and the righting lever pulls it back, so it overshoots and swings: that is roll. The swing is centred on the balance point, wherever list and heel have put it.

Offshore decision

Stability booklets and tow approvals check heel (wind against the GZ curve) and list (loading) as steady cases, then check that the largest angle in waves, mean plus roll, stays clear of the . Seafastening is designed for the roll accelerations, not just the steady angle.

Misconception

"A tilted vessel in calm water has a list, so ballast the high side down." If the cause is loll, the vessel is unstable upright. Adding ballast to the high side can make it flop over to the other side, often further. The fix for loll is to lower G: remove slack tanks' free surface, fill low tanks starting on the low side, or remove weight high up.

13.2The same pattern on every axis

The split between a steady offset and an oscillation around it is not special to sideways tilt. Every one of the six motions from Module 7 has a steady counterpart with its own name, and a moored vessel adds a third, slow layer in between.

DirectionSteady part (calm water, or steady wind and current)Oscillating part (waves)What is checked
Sideways tilt, , Mean angle plus roll against the downflooding angle
Fore-and-aft tilt ("by the stern" or "by the head")Bow and stern drafts, slamming, propeller immersion
Up and down from loading; when weight is added; while moving in shallow waterUnder-keel clearance, deck wetness, air gap
Turning, , to the mean weatherTrack keeping, heading limits for DP and turret systems
Sideways and fore-and-aft (moored)Mean from steady wind, current and (minutes) and and (seconds)Total excursion against riser limits; line tension against breaking strength

Trim and pitch

fore-and-aft tilt

Trim is set by where weight sits along the hull and is quoted in metres: the difference between the drafts at bow and stern. Pitch is the wave-driven swing around it, quoted in degrees. A barge trimmed by the stern pitches around that trimmed attitude, so its bow comes out of the water sooner. See Module 5.

Draft, sinkage, squat and heave

up and down

Draft is the depth of the keel at rest. Sinkage is a change in draft, usually from adding weight (or from squat). is the extra sinkage of a vessel moving through shallow water, and disappears when it stops. Heave is the wave-driven bobbing on top. See Modules 3 and 8.

Heading, crab and yaw

turning

Heading is where the bow points; track is where the vessel goes. The crab angle between them is held steadily against a cross-current or the wind's sideways push (leeway); see topic 8.3. A turret-moored FPSO weathervanes to a heading set by the mean weather. Yaw is the swing around any of these. See Modules 6 and 8.

Mean offset, slow drift and wave-frequency motion

a moored vessel's position

The mean offset is where the moorings balance the steady loads. Slow drift is a large, slow surge or sway at the mooring system's natural period, often one to three minutes. Wave-frequency motion follows each wave. A mooring analysis reports all three, and the total. See Module 11.

13.3Static versus dynamic loads

Forces follow the same pattern as motions. A crane, a mooring line or a hull girder carries a static load that is there in calm water, plus a dynamic load that comes and goes with the waves. The two usually have separate names, and a check that uses only the static name has missed the part that breaks things.

ItemStatic or steady nameDynamic nameHow they are combined
Crane liftStatic : the load plus riggingDynamic hook loadStatic ×
Mooring line, then mean tension under steady weatherDynamic tension; if the line goes slackMean + dynamic, against with a safety factor
TowlineMean towline tension (tow resistance)Peak tension in wavesSized for the peak, see Module 8
Hull girder from the loadingAdded, in both and
Analysis or analysis analysisStatic sets up the mean; dynamic finds the peaks and fatigue cycles

Why the names matter

A static load can be found from weights and geometry alone. A dynamic load needs motions, accelerations and time, which means a different analysis and different inputs (sea state, periods, damping). Separate names keep it clear which analysis a number came from and whether the dynamic part has been included yet.

Offshore decision

Lift plans state the static hook load, the DAF used and the crane's capacity at the working radius. Mooring reports give pretension, mean tension and maximum dynamic tension separately. Loading computers on FPSOs and barges track still-water bending moment continuously, because it is the part the crew can change by moving cargo or ballast.

Misconception

"The crane is rated for 500 t and the module weighs 450 t, so the lift is fine." Offshore, the crane and the load both move. A DAF of 1.2 to 1.3 is common, so the peak load is 540 to 585 t. The rated capacity at the working radius must cover the dynamic hook load, plus the rigging.

13.4One word, several statistics

"Wave height" and "wave period" sound like single numbers, but a real sea is a jumble of waves of every size. A forecast or a design report gives a statistic of that jumble, and different statistics of the same sea differ by a factor of two. Module 6 introduced the irregular sea; here the statistics are laid side by side.

H, Hs and Hmax

metres, trough to crest

H is one wave's height. , the significant wave height, is close to the average of the highest third of the waves and is what forecasts mean by "a 4 m sea". is the biggest wave in a stated duration, typically 1.8 to 2 times Hs in a 3-hour storm.

Tp and Tz

seconds

, the peak period, is the period carrying the most energy. , the mean zero-crossing period, is the average time between waves. For a typical wind sea Tz is about 0.7 to 0.8 of Tp. Reports use both, so check which one a resonance check uses.

Crest height

metres above still water

Air gap and green water checks need how high the crest rises, not the trough-to-crest height. In steep seas the crest is more than half the height, often around 60%.

Return period

years

A "100-year wave" is not a wave that arrives once a century. It has a 1% chance of being exceeded in any one year, and that chance builds up over a structure's life.

13.5Where it is measured from

Many vertical distances are just the gaps between a few reference levels: the keel, the waterline, the deck, the seabed, a tidal datum and a wave crest. Each gap has its own name. The same seabed can have three different "depths" depending on which water level it is measured from.

TermFromToNotes
KeelWaterlineChanges with loading; differs at bow and stern when trimmed
WaterlineDeck edgeDraft + freeboard = moulded depth
KeelMain deckA fixed dimension of the hull; "depth" here has nothing to do with the water
KeelSeabedWater depth − draft, then less squat, heave, pitch and roll
A water level (state which)SeabedCharts give depth below LAT; metocean and structural reports often use MSL
——Tidal reference levels: lowest astronomical tide, mean sea level, highest astronomical tide
Highest wave crest (including tide and surge)Underside of the lowest deckA key check for fixed platforms and semi-submersibles
and ——G is a point; KG is its height above the keel. KB and KM follow the same rule

The same trap exists for speed. and differ by the current: resistance and towline pull depend on the first, arrival time on the second (Module 8, topic 8.3).

13.6Mass, force and volume

Several words that sound like weights are not. Displacement, lightship and deadweight are masses. Gross and net tonnage are measures of volume. And "tonnes" is used loosely for force as well as mass: bollard pull, crane capacity and line strength are forces, often quoted in tonnes when what is meant is tonnes-force. Module 3 (topic 3.3) covers displacement and tonnage; this topic adds the unit traps. Units and conversions has every unit in the guide and a converter.

TermWhat it measuresUsual unitWatch out for
Mass of the whole floating vessel and contentsTonnesChanges with every load, ballast and fuel change
Mass of the empty vesselTonnesGrows over the vessel's life as equipment is added
Mass the vessel can carry at a given draftTonnesIncludes ballast, fuel and stores, not just cargo
Enclosed volumeDimensionlessNot a weight at all; it descends from the old register ton of 100 cubic feet
Mass: 1,000 kgtAlso called a metric ton; different from US and UK tons
Force: the weight of one tonnetf, often written just "t"Bollard pull, crane capacity and MBL are forces even when written in tonnes
ForcekNAbout one tenth of a tonne-force; mixing the two is a factor-of-ten error

13.7Names that depend on the job

The last family is simpler: the same kind of object gets a different name depending on what it does or where it is. Knowing the name tells you the job, and so which analysis and which standard apply.

Lines and ropesJob
Connects a tug to its tow
Y-shaped split at the towed end, spreading the pull to two points on the barge
A spare line rigged on the tow so it can be reconnected if the main towline breaks
Holds a floating unit to anchors on the seabed, usually chain, wire or polyester in sections
Heavy rope between two vessels or to a buoy, such as a shuttle tanker behind an FPSO
Wire or fibre loop connecting a lifted load to the crane hook
Pipes and cablesWhere and what
The section rising from the seabed to the vessel or platform; moves with the vessel
On the seabed within a field, between wells, manifolds and riser bases
A short pipe spool connecting two pieces of subsea equipment
Carries processed oil or gas out of the field to shore or another facility
A bundle of control, power and chemical lines, not production fluid
The outer pipe of a well, running down through a fixed platform into the seabed
Kinds of analysisWhat it means
and Steady loads only; quasi-static treats a varying load as if it were steady at each instant, ignoring inertia
Motion through time, including inertia and damping
Works wave period by wave period using RAOs; fast, but linear. AQWA's diffraction results are of this kind
Steps through a simulated storm second by second; slower, but handles slack lines, contact and other non-linear effects. OrcaFlex usually works this way
and Whole system, coarsely; then one detail, finely, using the global loads as input

What you should now understand

  • Most families split into a steady part with one name and an oscillation with another: list and heel against roll, trim against pitch, draft and squat against heave, mean offset against drift and wave-frequency motion.
  • Oscillations happen around the steady value, not around zero, so the extreme is the steady part plus the swing.
  • Loads work the same way: static hook load against DAF, pretension against dynamic tension, still-water against wave bending moment.
  • Hs, Hmax, Tp and Tz are different statistics of the same sea; a return period is a yearly probability, not a schedule.
  • Vertical terms are gaps between reference levels: always ask which level a depth or height is measured from.
  • "Tonnes" can mean mass or force, tonnage is volume, and kN against tonnes is a factor of about ten.
In practice

Engineering reports are precise about these words because each one points to a different load case, analysis or acceptance criterion. When reading one, it helps to ask three questions of any number: is it steady or dynamic, which statistic is it, and what is it measured from? The links each term to the others in its family.

Module 14 · Applied

Real vessels: the concepts in steel

Eight well-known vessels, each built around one or two of the ideas in this guide. For each one: a model drawing to scale, its main particulars, and the design decisions those particulars reveal. Read them as worked examples: every number is there because of a reason you have met before.

The question

A container ship, a barge and an offshore crane vessel all float, all carry weight, all meet the same waves. Why do they end up with such different shapes and proportions?

14.1Eight vessels at one scale

The line-up below puts every vessel in this module side by side at the same scale, each floating at a typical draught. Click a vessel to jump to its page. Notice how little the length tells you: the 91 m barge and the 89 m tug are almost the same length and could hardly be more different, and the wind turbine standing on the right is taller than most of the ships are long.

Stable by width

barge · Ever Given · Prelude · Pioneering Spirit

A wide waterplane makes BM large (BM = I ÷ volume, and I grows with beam cubed). Ships and barges rely on this form stability. The catch: a wide waterplane is also a stiff spring, so they respond to ordinary wave periods.

Stable by spread-out columns

Sleipnir · BOKA Vanguard (submerged)

A semi-submersible pierces the surface with a few columns placed far apart. Little waterplane area, so heave is soft and slow; but the area sits far from the centreline, so the second moment I, and with it GM, stays useful.

Stable by low weight

Hywind spar

A spar has almost no waterplane at all. It stays upright because heavy ballast puts G below B: it hangs like a pendulum. Very gentle motions, but it needs deep water.

Held by something else

tug · moorings · DP

Floating is only half the job. Each vessel also needs a way to stay put or move: engines and propellers, a tug and towline, mooring lines, or thrusters under computer control. That choice shapes the hull as much as stability does.

14.2A North Sea deck barge: the simplest hull that works

The workhorse of offshore transport is a flat steel box with no engine. The "300 ft" class is one of the most common sizes; the figures here are from a published datasheet for a pair of such barges built in 2013, 91.44 × 30.48 × 6.1 m (300 × 100 × 20 ft). It is close to the barge in the case study, and nearly everything about it is a direct answer to Modules 3 to 8.

Length × beam × depth
91.44 × 30.48 × 6.10 m
Loaded draught
4.89 m
Deadweight
10,866 t
Deck strength
25 t/m² (about 2.5 bar)
Ballast pumps
750 + 500 m³/h
Towing gear MBL

Design decisionWhyConcept
Wide, shallow boxBM = B² ÷ 12T = 30.48² ÷ (12 × 4.89) ≈ 15.8 m, so M sits about 18.3 m above the keel. Tall, heavy cargo can raise G well above the deck and GM stays large.Module 4
Low freeboard (1.2 m loaded)Depth costs steel and buys little for a box that only carries cargo on deck. But it limits the range: the deck edge goes under at only about 4.5°, and the GZ curve peaks soon after. Big GM, short range.Module 4, case study
Stiff in rollWith a GM of 10 m the roll period is about 0.8 × 30.48 ÷ √10 ≈ 7.7 s: short, inside the band of common wave periods. High stability means snappy rolling and large accelerations on the cargo, which the seafastening must carry.Module 7, 7.4
Raked bow and stern, skegs aftRakes cut tow resistance compared with a square end; the skegs give directional stability so the barge follows the tug instead of sheering from side to side.Module 8, 9.3
Deck rated 25 t/m², closely stiffenedCargo loads arrive as concentrated loads through a grillage. The rating (about 245 kN/m²) and the frame spacing tell engineers where the grillage must land.Module 10
Two longitudinal bulkheads, many tanksSubdivision for damage stability, and small tanks for trim and heel control with little free-surface loss. One metre of draught is about 2,860 t, so the 1,250 m³/h of pumps need over two hours for it: load-out plans are built around that rate and the tide.Module 5, 2.3
Towing gear with 2,270 kN MBLThe bridle and brackets must be stronger than the tug can pull. With the usual factor of about 2.2 on bollard pull, this gear suits tugs up to about 105 t bollard pull without restriction.13.6, Module 8

14.3Ever Given: a 400 m container ship in a canal

One of the Evergreen G-class, the largest container ships of their day. On 23 March 2021 she ran aground across the Suez Canal in strong wind and blowing sand, and blocked it for six days. Her proportions explain both why she is economical and why a canal is a hard place for her.

Length × beam
399.94 × 58.8 m
Depth
32.9 m
Draught (design / max)
14.5 / 16.0 m
Deadweight
≈ 199,600 t
Capacity
20,124 TEU
Engine · speed
59,300 kW · ~22.8 kn
Design decisionWhyConcept
Long and slender (L/B ≈ 6.8)Wave-making resistance depends on length; a long hull makes smaller waves at a given speed. One engine and one propeller move 20,000 boxes.Module 8, 9.1
Wide beam (58.8 m)Containers stack high on deck, which raises G. Beam buys back stability (BM grows with B²), and 24 rows of boxes fit across.Module 4
Modest GM, by intentToo much GM means violent rolling and lashing failures. With GM of about 2 m the roll period is roughly 33 s. That slow roll invites in long head or following seas, when the wave encounter period is about half the roll period.Module 7, Module 12
Bulbous bowIts own wave cancels part of the bow wave at the design speed and draught.9.2
Bridge forward, engine aft ("twin island")From an aft bridge, the officers could not see the water ahead over the stacks. Moving the bridge forward meets the visibility rules and frees space aft for more boxes.Module 2
Huge side area above waterAbout 14,000 m² of hull and boxes (estimate). A 35 kn wind pushes with roughly 2.8 MN, about 280 tonnes-force, and the hull's grip on the water is weak at canal speeds.Module 8, Module 13
Deep draught in a shallow canalSquat by the ICORELS formula: about 0.3 m at 8 kn, 0.6 m at 12 kn in 24 m of water, and more in a narrow, confined channel. Near a bank, the flow between hull and bank pulls the stern in: bank effect.8.5

What the Suez grounding shows

The flag state's investigation found the pilots and master had not properly evaluated the strong wind and poor visibility, and that tugs were not used to help control the ship. The physics in the table are all ordinary: wind on a huge side area, weak steering at low speed, squat and bank effect in a confined channel. Together they used up the margin.

The link to offshore work

The same arithmetic, wind area times wind pressure against the forces available to resist it, decides whether a tug can hold a barge carrying a tall module (Module 8) and whether a moored vessel stays within its offset limits (Module 11).

Misconception

"A bigger ship is a safer ship." Bigger brings more inertia and better seakeeping in open water, but more wind area, less clearance in channels and slower responses to rudder and engine. Size moves the risks; it does not remove them.

14.4Prelude FLNG: a ship that never sails

The largest floating offshore facility built: a 488 m hull that liquefies natural gas about 200 km off Western Australia and stores it until carriers collect it. It has no propulsion engine; it was towed to site in 2017 and is meant to stay there for 25 years, through Category 5 cyclones. It belongs to the family: a ship-shaped hull chosen for storage volume, held by a turret mooring.

Design decisionWhyConcept
A ship-shaped hull, not a semi or a sparIt must store large volumes of LNG and liquids between offloadings; a long box hull gives storage volume and deck space for the gas plant cheaply.9.5
Draught from displacement600,000 t ÷ (1.025 t/m³ × 488 × 74 m) ≈ 16 m if the hull were a perfect box; real ends are finer, so it floats a little deeper.Module 3
Internal turret near the bowThe hull weathervanes around the turret, so it always meets the weather bow-on: smallest wind, wave and current loads, and less roll. The non-turning chain table stays connected to the moorings and risers.Module 6, Module 11
Quarters at the bow, flare at the sternBecause the bow points into the wind, gas leaks and flare heat blow away from the living quarters.11.1
16 lines on driven pilesLines grouped four by four so the system still holds with a line broken; piles 65 m long take the loads in the seabed soil.Module 11
Tank shape against sloshingLiquid cargo held at any fill level sloshes as the hull moves. Partially filled tanks are a free-surface and structural problem that land-based plants never face.5.2

14.5BOKA Vanguard: a ship that sinks its own deck

A semi-submersible , built in 2012 to carry the largest floating platforms in one piece. She ballasts down until her deck is 16 m under water, the cargo floats in over it, and she deballasts to lift it dry. Her first cargo was the Jack/St. Malo semi-submersible hull, about 53,000 t; she has also carried an FPSO and a 193 m spar hull.

Length × deck width
275 × 70 m
Draught: sailing / submerged
11 / 31 m
Deck under water
up to 16 m
Deadweight
≈ 117,000 t
Cargo
up to ~110,000 t
Bow
none: open deck end to end
Design decisionWhyConcept
No forecastle, flat deck end to endCargo can be wider and longer than the deck and overhang it. The deck is watertight and is meant to have sea washing over it.Module 2
Huge ballast capacitySinking a 70 m wide deck 16 m under water means taking on tens of thousands of tonnes of water. Above the deck, each metre of draught is about 19,700 t of ballast (275 × 70 m box).Module 5, 2.3
Buoyancy casings at the deck edgesWhen the deck goes under, the waterplane collapses to whatever still pierces the surface. Casings far out to the sides keep a waterplane with a useful second moment, so the vessel stays stable while submerged. They can be moved to suit each cargo.Module 4, 9.5
Deckhouse at one sideKeeps the full width clear for cargo, and its own volume adds waterplane during the submerged stage.Module 4
Very wide (70 m) for her lengthLarge GM with a tall, heavy cargo on deck. Like the barge, she then rolls quickly, so cargo seafastening is designed for the motions of the voyage.7.4

14.6Sleipnir: a semi-submersible crane vessel

The largest crane vessel when delivered in 2019: two revolving cranes of 10,000 t each on a semi-submersible hull, running on LNG. In September 2019 the two cranes together lifted a 15,300 t topsides module at the Leviathan gas field, a record for a crane vessel. She changes from a ship to a platform and back by ballasting.

Length × width
220 × 102 m
Draught
12 to 32 m
Cranes
2 × 10,000 t
Hull
2 pontoons, 8 columns
Ballast pumps
8 × 3,250 m³/h
Record lift
15,300 t (2019)
Design decisionWhyConcept
Semi-submersible hullAt operating draught only the columns cut the surface: a small waterplane, so a soft heave spring and natural periods well above most wave periods. Small motions are what make a 10,000 t lift possible offshore.9.5, Module 7
Two draughts: ~12 m transit, deeper to workFloating on the pontoons she has little drag and a big waterplane, so she sails efficiently. Ballasted down, she becomes a steady platform. The designers kept the pontoon draught shallow enough to moor at her shore base.Module 5
Eight columns, mid columns widened at the topMany columns let waves pass between them. Similar column areas avoid coupling heave and pitch in long swell; extra area at the mid columns adds waterplane and stability for the heaviest tandem lifts.Module 4, Module 7
Cranes at the sternThe load goes over the stern, away from the accommodation, with the whole hull length behind it to reach over a platform.5.3
26,000 m³/h of ballast pumpsFour pump rooms, each with two 3,250 m³/h pumps: about four hours to operating draught. During a lift, ballast is moved to keep her level as the load comes on and the crane slews; boom angle limits are only a few degrees.5.3, 2.3
Column height set by survival crestsThe deckbox must stay clear of the highest wave crests in a storm: the air gap.13.5

Why ballast is the vessel's life support

A semi-submersible's ballast system is not a convenience. It sets draught, trim, heel and stability through every stage of a lift, and a fault in it can flood the hull.

A warning from the same family

In July 2005 the semi-submersible platform Thunder Horse was evacuated for Hurricane Dennis and was found listing heavily afterwards. The investigation found that ballast water had moved into manned spaces in the lower hull through faulty and wrongly installed check valves, and then spread through openings that should have been watertight. No hull breach: the ballast and bilge piping alone flooded her.

Design response

Ballast systems on column-stabilised units get independent valve control, check valves that are verified in place, watertight integrity checks of every pipe and cable through each bulkhead, and stability calculations for an accidentally flooded compartment.

14.7Pioneering Spirit: lifting a whole platform at once

A twin-hulled vessel built to install or remove complete platform topsides in a single lift, by straddling the platform with a slot cut into her bow. She removed Shell's Brent Delta topsides (24,200 t) in 2017, and Brent Charlie (31,000 t) in 2024, a record for an offshore lift. She also lays pipelines, and lifts jackets with beams over her stern.

Length × beam
382 × 124 m (477 m with beams)
Draught
10 to 27 m
Displacement
365,000 t transit, ~932,000 t max
Topsides lift
48,000 t (60,000 t upgrade)
Jacket lift
20,000 t
Station-keeping
DP3, 12 thrusters, ~95 MW
Design decisionWhyConcept
Lift by deballasting, not by craneBuoyancy does the lifting. Pumping out ballast makes the hull rise and carry the topsides on the beams: the same principle as a float-over, run in reverse. 31,000 t on beams would sink her about 0.75 m if no ballast went out.1.6, Module 5
Slot between two bowsA crane must reach over and hang the load. Straddling the platform puts the load inside the hull's footprint instead: no outreach, no boom limits, and the lift rating is about 5% of her maximum displacement.5.3
Very wide (124 m)Each half-hull must stay stable with half a platform's weight on its inner edge, and the whole vessel has huge waterplane stiffness. The hull was widened by 6.75 m during construction to give more room around platform legs.Module 4
Motion-compensated lifting beamsThe vessel moves in waves, the platform does not. The beams absorb the relative motion and then lift the load clear quickly, so it is never struck twice.Module 7, case study
Dynamic positioning, DP3No anchors among pipelines and platform legs. DP3 means any single failure, including fire or flood in one compartment, leaves enough thrusters to hold position.Module 11

14.8Hywind Scotland: a floating wind turbine on a spar

The first commercial floating wind farm, switched on in 2017 about 25 km off Peterhead: five 6 MW turbines, each on a single steel spar that floats upright in 95 to 120 m of water. A spar is the most extreme answer in this module to "how do you stay upright?"

Spar hull
91 m long, 14.5 m across
Draught
~78 m
Mass ballasted
> 10,000 t (2,300 t steel)
Turbine
6 MW, rotor 154 m
Mooring
3 chains, suction anchors
Height above water
~175 to 178 m to blade tip
Design decisionWhyConcept
Deep, ballasted cylinderThe turbine's mass and the rotor thrust act very high up. A waterplane cannot resist that: BM here is at most about 0.2 m. Instead, rock and water ballast at the bottom put G below B, so any tilt is righted like a pendulum.1.1, Module 4
Slender where it cuts the surfaceA small waterplane is a soft heave spring, so heave and pitch natural periods sit well above wave periods. Motion at the nacelle stays small.9.5
Three slack catenary linesThe spar may drift a little in surge and sway; the moorings only stop it wandering. Three lines at 120° hold from every direction.Module 11
Suction anchorsLarge open-bottomed steel cans sucked into the seabed: quick to install, and they resist both horizontal and some vertical pull.Module 11
Turbine control tuned for a floating baseA normal turbine controller, pitching its blades as the wind changes, can feed energy into the tower's fore-and-aft rocking. The control is changed so it damps the motion instead of driving it.Module 7
Assembled in a deep fjordWith a 78 m draught, the spar cannot come to a normal quay. The turbines were fitted in sheltered deep water in Norway and the complete units towed to Scotland.Module 8

14.9ALP Striker: an ocean towing tug

One of four long-haul towing and anchor-handling tugs built in Japan around 2016–17 for ocean towage of rigs and FPSOs. On sea trials she recorded 309.6 t of bollard pull, and she carries fuel to tow at full power for 45 days. A tug is the opposite of a barge: little cargo, a great deal of power, and a hull shaped around one line at the stern.

Length × beam
88.9 × 21 m
Max draught
8.5 m
Bollard pull (trials)
309.6 t
Speed
13 kn service, 19 kn max
Endurance
45 days towing at full power
Winch
3 drums, 400 t
Design decisionWhyConcept
Deep draught for her sizeBollard pull comes from propellers pushing water. Deep propellers stay immersed in waves and keep their grip; a tug that pitches its propellers out of the water loses thrust when it is most needed.Module 8
Low, long aft deck with a stern rollerThe towline and anchor wires leave the vessel low and on the centreline, over a roller, so pull acts with the smallest heeling lever.1.1
High bow, superstructure forwardKeeps green water off the forward deck while heading into weather with a tow; the wheelhouse faces aft so the master can watch the line.Module 2
Protection against girtingIf the tow sheers out to the side, a towline pulling abeam at deck level can roll the tug over in seconds. Gog ropes hold the line aft, the towing point is kept low, and the hook or winch has an emergency release.Module 4
Tug and tow gear must matchHer 310 t of pull would need towing gear with an MBL near 680 t at the usual factor; the barge in 14.2 has 231 t. The weakest link must be chosen before the tow, not discovered during it.13.6, 14.2

Particulars are from builders', owners' and operators' published specifications and widely reported figures; sources differ slightly, and ratings change with upgrades. Derived numbers (BM, roll period, wind force, squat, sinkage) use the guide's simple formulas and are estimates for understanding, not for design.

What you should now understand

  • Every vessel's proportions trace back to its job: carry, lift, store, tow or hold still.
  • Width buys stability (BM grows with beam squared) but makes a stiff, quick-rolling hull; a small waterplane buys gentle motion but needs another source of stability.
  • Three ways to stay upright: a wide waterplane, columns spread far apart, or G below B.
  • Ballast is a design tool: it turns a ship into a platform (Sleipnir), sinks a deck (BOKA Vanguard) or lifts a platform (Pioneering Spirit).
  • Moving or holding a vessel is its own design problem: engines, tugs and towlines, turrets and moorings, or DP.
In practice

When a report names a vessel, look up its main particulars first: length, beam, depth, draught, displacement and lightship. With the formulas in this guide, those six numbers already tell you roughly how stiff it is in roll, how deep it sits, how much ballast a change of draught takes and how much wind it catches. The detailed analysis then refines what the particulars predict.

Guided case study

Can we safely tow a loaded barge and install its offshore payload?

A 2,500 t topside module must travel about 400 nautical miles on a 90 m transport barge, then be lifted onto a jacket by a crane vessel. Walk through the questions an engineering team would ask, in roughly the order they would ask them. Each step reuses a model from the modules.

This is a way of connecting concepts, not a procedure. A real assessment uses the actual barge, cargo, route and metocean data, a validated analysis, the governing standards and independent review by a marine warranty surveyor. The numbers here come from the guide's simplified models.

Quick reference

Units and conversions

Offshore engineering works in metric (SI) units, plus a few sea-going ones such as knots and nautical miles, and some habits of its own: forces quoted in tonnes, pressures in bar, angles in degrees. Older drawings and US documents add feet, pounds and short tons. This page collects every unit the guide uses, with the conversions that matter when reading a report.

QuantityUnits you will seeConversions and a feel for the sizeWhere
Masst (tonne), kg; lb, short ton, long ton1 t = 1,000 kg ≈ 2,205 lb. A US short ton is 2,000 lb = 0.907 t; a UK long ton is 2,240 lb = 1.016 t.13.6
Force and weightkN, MN, N; "t" meaning tonnes-force (tf)1 tf = the weight of 1 t = 9.81 kN, roughly 10 kN. 1 MN = 1,000 kN ≈ 102 tf. Bollard pull, crane capacity and line strength are forces even when written in tonnes.13.6
Momentt·m (tonne-metres), kN·m, MN·mMoment = force × lever arm. 1 t·m = 9.81 kN·m. 100 t at 10 m and 50 t at 20 m are both 1,000 t·m.1.1, 10
Pressurebar, kPa, MPa, psi; metres of head1 bar = 100 kPa = 0.1 MPa ≈ 14.5 psi ≈ 10 m of seawater. The atmosphere is about 1.013 bar. "barg" is gauge pressure (above the atmosphere), "bara" is absolute.1.2
StressMPa = N/mm²; ksi in US documents1 MPa = 10 bar ≈ 145 psi; 1 ksi = 1,000 psi ≈ 6.9 MPa. Common structural steel (S355) yields at about 355 MPa.10
Densityt/m³, kg/m³1 t/m³ = 1,000 kg/m³. Seawater 1.025, fresh water 1.000, crude oil about 0.85, steel 7.85 t/m³.1.2
Lengthm, cm, mm; ft, in1 ft = 0.3048 m; 1 in = 25.4 mm. Drafts and waves in metres, small draft changes in centimetres, plate thickness in millimetres.3
Distance at seanautical mile (nm or NM)1 nautical mile = 1,852 m, one minute of latitude, about 1.15 land miles.8
Area and volumem², m³; barrels (bbl) for oil1 m³ of seawater weighs 1.025 t. 1 barrel = 0.159 m³, so 1 m³ ≈ 6.29 bbl; an FPSO storing 1 million barrels holds about 159,000 m³.3
ImmersionTPC (tonnes per centimetre)Tonnes needed to sink the hull 1 cm deeper: water density × waterplane area ÷ 100. A 90 m × 27 m barge in seawater: about 25 t/cm.3
Speedkn (knots), m/s, km/h1 kn = 1 nautical mile per hour = 0.514 m/s = 1.852 km/h; 1 m/s ≈ 1.94 kn. Vessel and current speeds are usually in knots, wind often in m/s.8
Accelerationm/s², gg = 9.81 m/s². An acceleration of "0.2 g" is 1.96 m/s², and pushes on cargo with 20% of its weight.7
Time and periods, hWave, roll and heave periods in seconds; sea-state statistics usually over 3 hours; return periods in years.6
FrequencyHz, rad/sFrequency (Hz) = 1 ÷ period; angular frequency (rad/s) = 2π ÷ period. A 10 s period is 0.1 Hz or 0.63 rad/s. RAO plots may use any of the three on the horizontal axis.7.2
Angledegrees (°), radians1 radian = 57.3°. Heel, trim and roll angles are in degrees; trim is also often given as the difference in drafts, in metres.4, 5
Line weightkg/m, kN/m (submerged)Chain, wire and pipe are specified by mass per metre; the catenary shape depends on the submerged weight per metre (about 13% less for steel).11
Prefixesk, M, G; mk = thousand, M = million, G = thousand million. A lower-case m in front of a unit means thousandth (mm); on its own it means metres. MN and mN differ by a factor of a thousand million.

Tonnes or kilonewtons?

factor of about 10

A figure in kN is about ten times the same figure in tonnes. Reading 800 kN as 800 t overstates a pull tenfold; reading 80 t as 80 kN understates it tenfold. Always check the unit before comparing a load with a capacity.

Which ton?

2% to 10% apart

Tonne (1,000 kg), long ton (1,016 kg) and short ton (907 kg) are close enough to be confused and far enough apart to matter. US crane and rigging data are often in short tons.

Gauge or absolute?

1 bar apart

Gauge pressure starts from the atmosphere, absolute pressure from a vacuum. The difference is 1 bar, which is small at 150 bar on the seabed but large in a tank test at 0.25 bar.

Hz or rad/s?

factor of 2π ≈ 6.3

Check the axis label on any RAO or spectrum plot. A resonance at "0.63" is a 10 s period in rad/s but a 1.6 s period in Hz.

Height or amplitude?

factor of 2

Wave height is crest to trough; amplitude is half of it. An RAO is usually motion amplitude per metre of wave amplitude, and "single" or "double amplitude" in a report means half or the whole of the swing.

Knots or m/s?

factor of about 2

A 20 m/s wind is about 39 kn. Wind loads grow with speed squared, so mixing the two up changes a force about fourfold.

Quick reference

Rules of thumb

Numbers worth remembering when reading reports or sanity-checking a result. They are approximations from the guide's simple models and standard references, good for spotting a figure that is wildly off, not for design.

TopicRule of thumbWhere
Weight and force1 tonne weighs about 9.81 kN, so roughly 10 kN. A figure in kN is about ten times the same figure in tonnes.13.6
DensitiesSeawater 1.025 t/m³, fresh water 1.000, steel 7.85. A vessel floats about 2.5% deeper in fresh water.1.2
PressureEvery 10 m of seawater adds about 1 bar (100 kPa, about 10 t on each square metre).1.2
Walls and bulkheadsDouble the depth of liquid against a wall: four times the force, eight times the bending at its base.1.4
Weight in waterSolid steel loses about 13% of its weight under water. Anything with trapped air may float.1.6
Centre of gravityG = Σ(weight × position) ÷ total weight. A load's effect is its weight × its distance from the reference.1.1
StabilityInitial stability needs G below the metacentre M (positive GM). For a box hull BM = beam² ÷ (12 × draft), so stability grows with beam squared.4
Roll periodAbout 2π × 0.4 × beam ÷ √(g × GM): high GM gives a short, snappy roll; low GM a slow one.4
Hull fullnessBlock coefficient about 1.0 for a box barge, 0.85 bulk carrier, 0.6 container ship, 0.55 tug.9.1
Wave length and speedDeep water: wavelength ≈ 1.56 × period² (m), crest speed ≈ 1.56 × period (m/s), about 3 × period in knots. A 10 s wave is about 156 m long.6.1
Wind-made wavesFully developed sea: peak period ≈ 0.8 × wind speed (m/s), Hs ≈ 0.025 × wind speed². Double the wind, double the period, four times the height. Swell crosses 1,000 km in about 22 h at 16 s.6.4
Wave motion with depthHalf a wavelength down, water motion is only about 4% of that at the surface. Wave energy travels at half the crest speed in deep water.6.2
CurrentsWind drives a surface current of about 2% of the wind speed, gone by about 50 m down. Tidal currents reverse about every 6 hours and are nearly uniform with depth. Current drag grows with speed squared: 1 kn to 2 kn is four times the push.6.5
Wave statisticsMean wave ≈ 0.6 × Hs; largest in a 3-hour storm ≈ 1.8–2 × Hs. Tz ≈ 0.7–0.8 × Tp. Waves break at a steepness of about 1 : 7.13.4
Return periodsA 100-year event has about a 22% chance of happening at least once in 25 years, and about 63% in 100 years.13.4
ResonanceMotions are largest when the wave period is close to the vessel's natural period. Small waterplane for its volume (semi-submersible, spar) means a long heave period, clear of most waves.7, 9.5
Resistance and squatBoth grow roughly with speed squared: double the speed, about four times the towing force; halve the speed, about a quarter of the squat.8
Speed and distance1 knot = 0.514 m/s = 1.852 km/h; 1 nautical mile = 1,852 m.8
BeamsHalve the depth of a beam and its bending stress roughly quadruples; deflection grows even faster.10
LiftsOffshore lifts typically use a dynamic amplification factor of 1.1–1.3 on top of the static hook load.13.3
MooringsTension rises steeply with offset as the catenary lifts off the seabed; total excursion = mean offset + slow drift + wave-frequency motion.11, 13.2

Further reading

Reading and references

The explanations in this guide follow standard textbook treatments. Start with Tupper; go to the others when you want depth on a specific topic.

  1. Tupper, E. C. Introduction to Naval Architecture, 5th ed. Butterworth-Heinemann, 2013.Primary introductory reference: flotation, stability, resistance, seakeeping and strength in accessible form. Modules 3 to 5, 7, 8 and 10.
  2. Rawson, K. J. and Tupper, E. C. Basic Ship Theory, 5th ed., 2 vols. Butterworth-Heinemann, 2001.The fuller treatment behind Tupper's introduction.
  3. Biran, A. and López-Pulido, R. Ship Hydrostatics and Stability, 2nd ed. Butterworth-Heinemann, 2014.Large-angle stability, GZ curves, free surface and stability criteria (Modules 4 and 5).
  4. Journée, J. M. J. and Massie, W. W. Offshore Hydromechanics. Delft University of Technology, 2001 (open textbook).Waves, added mass, damping, RAOs, spectra, moorings and resistance, written for offshore engineers (Modules 6 to 8 and 11).
  5. Faltinsen, O. M. Sea Loads on Ships and Offshore Structures. Cambridge University Press, 1990.The standard graduate text on wave loads and motions.
  6. Holthuijsen, L. H. Waves in Oceanic and Coastal Waters. Cambridge University Press, 2007.Wave statistics, spectra and significant wave height (Module 6).
  7. Chakrabarti, S. K. (ed.) Handbook of Offshore Engineering. Elsevier, 2005.Broad reference on floating systems, moorings, risers and installation (Module 11).
  8. DNV. DNV-ST-N001 Marine operations and marine warranty.Load-out, transport, towing, lifting, weather-restricted operations and forecast factors (Modules 5, 8, 12 and the case study).
  9. DNV. DNV-RP-C205 Environmental conditions and environmental loads; DNV-RP-C203 Fatigue design of offshore steel structures.Metocean description and loads; S–N curves and fatigue methods (Modules 6 and 10).
  10. DNV. DNV-OS-E301 Position mooring; API. RP 2SK Design and Analysis of Stationkeeping Systems for Floating Structures.Mooring design and analysis (Module 11).
  11. IMO. International Code on Intact Stability, 2008 (2008 IS Code).The regulatory framework for intact stability criteria (Module 4).
  12. Orcina OrcaFlex documentation; Ansys Aqwa theory and user manuals; Strand7 reference documentation.For each tool's axis conventions, RAO definitions and modelling assumptions when reading analysis results.
